scenarios.title: The prerequisite audit
scenarios.situation: A sophomore asks you how to prepare for quant internships. Their coursework so far: one semester of calculus, an intro stats class that never covered joint distributions, and a Python course focused on web scraping. They want to start grinding interview brainteasers immediately.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right first move?
choices: Audit and close the math gaps first — multivariable calculus, linear algebra, and probability through conditional expectation — before interview prep, because every quant interview question sits on top of that foundation.
Start with brainteasers; interview performance matters more than coursework depth.
Switch to a finance major immediately; the degree name is what recruiters screen for.
Learn C++ first; speed of implementation is the binding constraint.
scenarios.why: Quant interviews test probability, statistics, linear algebra, and calculus under time pressure. A student who cannot compute a conditional expectation or diagonalize a matrix will fail the interview regardless of how many puzzles they've memorized. The audit maps exactly which prerequisites are missing so study time goes to the binding constraint — the math, not the puzzles.
scenarios.hint: What do the brainteasers assume you already know?

scenarios.title: The internship map
scenarios.situation: A junior with strong math grades asks when to apply for quant trading and research internships. They assume the timeline matches regular software engineering recruiting — applications in the fall of junior year, interviews in winter — and plan to start preparing next summer.
scenarios.prompt: What should you tell them about the quant recruiting timeline?
choices: Quant recruiting runs much earlier than general SWE: applications and interviews for top firms typically happen in the summer and early fall, a full year before the internship — so preparation must start now, not next summer.
The timeline is identical to SWE; their plan is fine.
Internships don't matter for quant; only graduate school admissions do.
They should wait until senior year when they have more coursework.
scenarios.why: Quant funds and trading firms run accelerated, early pipelines — many interview in late summer/early fall for the following summer's internship. A junior who waits until the standard SWE timeline finds the quant seats already filled. The map matters because the preparation (probability depth, mental math, programming) must be done before the window opens, not during it.
scenarios.hint: If interviews happen a year before the internship, when must preparation be finished?

scenarios.title: Conditional expectation under pressure
scenarios.situation: In a mock interview you're asked: a fair coin is flipped until the first head appears. You are paid $2^n where n is the number of flips. Then a twist: you may stop the game at any time before the flip and take a fixed $3 instead. The interviewer wants the fair value of the game with the stop option.
scenarios.prompt: How do you reason about it?
choices: Compute the conditional expectation of continuing at each state: after k tails the expected remaining value doubles each flip while the stop value is fixed, so the optimal policy and the game's value come from comparing E[continue | k tails] against $3 at each decision point — the stop option is worth taking exactly when the conditional expectation of continuing falls below it.
The game is worth infinite dollars because the payoff is unbounded, so the stop option is irrelevant.
The value is $3 because you would always stop immediately.
Flip until the expected payoff exceeds $3, which happens on the first flip.
scenarios.why: This is an optimal-stopping problem in miniature: at each state you compare the conditional expectation of continuing against the certain $3. The naive 'infinite expectation' answer (the St. Petersburg paradox) ignores the decision structure; the interview tests whether you condition on the information you actually have at each decision point. Working the recursion — value at state k = max(3, expected value of flipping once more) — is the whole skill.
scenarios.hint: After one tail, what is the expected value of flipping exactly once more versus stopping?

scenarios.title: The vectorized backtest
scenarios.situation: A candidate shows you a backtest of a mean-reversion strategy written as a Python for-loop over 10 years of minute bars. It takes 40 minutes to run, so they tested 3 parameter sets. They ask whether to optimize the loop with C++.
scenarios.prompt: What is the more important fix?
choices: Vectorize the strategy with array operations (NumPy/pandas) so a run takes seconds, enabling hundreds of parameter trials — but first fix the methodology: the loop likely contains look-ahead bias (using information not available at trade time), which no amount of speed can rescue.
Rewrite in C++; speed is the binding constraint in quant research.
Test more parameter sets on the 40-minute loop; compute is cheap if you run it overnight.
The strategy is mean-reversion so the loop is fine; only high-frequency strategies need vectorization.
scenarios.why: Two problems, in order of importance: correctness, then speed. A 40-minute loop that peeks at future data produces a beautiful, worthless equity curve — look-ahead bias is the classic backtest killer. Once the logic is point-in-time correct, vectorization turns 40 minutes into seconds, which is what actually enables research velocity: the number of ideas you can test per day.
scenarios.hint: How would you check whether the loop uses future information?

scenarios.title: The proctored exam decision
scenarios.situation: You've completed the five graduate courses in an online MicroMasters-style finance credential: modern finance foundations, financial accounting, mathematical methods for quantitative finance, and derivatives markets. The final step is a single proctored comprehensive exam, and you're debating whether the exam is worth the stress and fee.
scenarios.prompt: How should you value the proctored exam?
choices: The verified credential — courses plus the proctored comprehensive exam — is what converts coursework into a signal employers and degree programs recognize; without the exam you have knowledge but no credential, and the degree-pathway value (advanced standing toward a master's) typically requires the full verified MicroMasters.
Skip the exam; the knowledge is what matters and employers never check credentials.
The exam only matters if you want to become a professor.
Retake the easiest course instead; a higher average grade signals more.
scenarios.why: Graduate-level online credentials derive their signaling value from verification: proctored exams prove the work is yours. The MicroMasters model explicitly ties the credential — and any credit or advanced-standing pathway into a master's program — to completing the verified track including the comprehensive exam. Skipping it keeps the learning but forfeits the signal and the pathway option.
scenarios.hint: What does the exam prove that the coursework alone doesn't?

scenarios.title: The career fork
scenarios.situation: A PhD student in applied math has three offers: desk quant at a bank (pricing and hedging exotics, close to trading), quantitative researcher at a fund (alpha research, longer horizons), and a strategy consulting role at a top firm (generalist problem-solving, client-facing). They love stochastic calculus and also love explaining ideas to non-technical audiences.
scenarios.prompt: How should they think about the fork?
choices: Map the roles to what they actually optimize: desk quant = deep derivatives math under trading-floor time pressure; researcher = open-ended statistical modeling with publication-like rigor and slower feedback; consultant = breadth, communication, and business judgment with less technical depth. The right choice follows which daily work — not which prestige — fits their strengths, and the consulting door stays open later than the quant doors.
Take the highest-paying offer; the work converges within two years anyway.
Take consulting; quants burn out and the math is the same everywhere.
Take the desk quant role; researchers never touch real markets.
scenarios.why: The three paths diverge in daily reality: desk quants live inside stochastic calculus and trader requests with intraday deadlines; researchers run longer experiments on noisy data where most ideas fail; consultants trade depth for breadth and client influence. Loving both the math and the explaining is real information — it points toward roles where technical depth meets communication (desk quant facing traders, or consulting with a quant edge) — and the fork is not permanent, but switching costs rise with seniority, so choose on work-content fit first.
scenarios.hint: What does a typical Tuesday look like in each role?
objectives: desk quant vs researcher vs consultant

scenarios.title: The Quantitative Finance: The Ladder Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Quantitative Finance: The Ladder is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Quantitative Finance: The Ladder?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Quantitative Finance: The Ladder issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Quantitative Finance: The Ladder is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Quantitative Finance: The Ladder supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Quantitative Finance: The Ladder failure in Quant Finance Ladder.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Quantitative Finance: The Ladder
evidence: All Quantitative Finance: The Ladder components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

domains.name: Start Here
domains.description: Orientation: how to use this bootcamp, study strategy, the course roadmap, and the lab environment.

scenarios.title: The Ladder's Order
scenarios.situation: A friend wants to skip to derivatives pricing ('the interesting part') without probability. You advise them.
choices: Don't: the dependency graph runs probability → stochastic processes → derivatives — Black-Scholes IS Itô's lemma applied, which IS conditional expectation in continuous time. Skipping ahead borrows confusion at interest; the 'interesting part' is incomprehensible without the foundation. Climb in order; the interesting part gets MORE interesting with the machinery to understand it.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The dependency is real, not pedagogical preference: risk-neutral pricing is a change of measure (Girsanov), the PDE comes from Itô's lemma, Greeks are Taylor expansions. Each is a probability concept in finance clothing. Students who skip arrive at Black-Scholes able to recite it and unable to derive, extend, or debug it — which is exactly what interviews test.
scenarios.hint: What is Black-Scholes made of, mathematically?
evidence: Derivatives = probability in finance clothing. Climb in order.

scenarios.title: The Passive Reader
scenarios.situation: A student reads every lesson twice and scores poorly on scenarios. Another does half the reading but all scenarios closed-book and scores well.
choices: Retrieval practice: closed-book scenarios force recall, which builds memory; re-reading builds familiarity (fluency illusion). The testing effect is the most replicated finding in learning science — active recall beats passive review by wide margins. The second student trained retrieval; the first trained recognition. Exams test retrieval.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The fluency illusion: re-read text feels known because recognition is easy — but exams demand recall, a different process. Closed-book scenario attempts, prediction-before-reading, and the error log are all retrieval practice. Study time is fixed; spend it on the activity with the highest transfer — attempting, failing, and correcting.
scenarios.hint: Recognition or recall — which do exams test?
evidence: Retrieval builds memory; recognition builds illusion.

scenarios.title: The Half Lab
scenarios.situation: A student 'reads' the Monte Carlo lab, understands it, but doesn't run the code. 'I get the idea,' they say.
choices: Procedural fluency: understanding the idea is declarative knowledge; the interview and the job need procedural — writing the sampler, debugging the sqrt(dt), interpreting the SE. The lab's checks are the fluency test: code that passes them is knowledge you can USE. 'Getting the idea' is the first 20%; the checks are the other 80%. The bugs you hit ARE the learning.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The declarative/procedural gap: you can understand importance sampling perfectly and still write the likelihood ratio upside-down — the lab catches it. Every quant interview includes implementation or whiteboard coding; 'I get the idea' doesn't compile. The checks define done: green checks = usable skill. The struggle with the code IS the learning, not an obstacle to it.
scenarios.hint: What do the lab checks actually test?
evidence: Ideas don't compile. Green checks = usable skill.

scenarios.title: The Repeated Mistake
scenarios.situation: A student confuses P(A|B) with P(B|A) in January, March, and again in May. Each time they 'relearn' it.
scenarios.prompt: What broke, and what fixes it?
choices: No error log: without a written record (concept, correction, re-test date), each mistake is learned from scratch — the same lesson paid for three times. The log converts errors into curriculum: write the confusion, the correct direction, a drill, and a re-test date. Spaced re-testing of logged errors is the highest-ROI study activity. Forgetting is the default; the log is the countermeasure.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The forgetting curve: without spaced retrieval, each 'relearning' starts near zero — three learnings, one retention. The log's re-test dates enforce the spacing that memory needs. The meta-point: the student's system, not their talent, failed — good systems beat good intentions. Every repeated error is a missing log entry.
scenarios.hint: How many times should one mistake be paid for?
evidence: Once paid, logged, re-tested. Forgetting is default; systems win.

domains.name: Capstone: Build a Quant Research Platform
domains.description: An end-to-end project: a derivatives pricing and backtesting platform — data, models, risk, and validation, built in phases.

scenarios.title: Picking the Strategy
scenarios.situation: For the capstone you must pick ONE strategy: skew trading, pairs trading, or vol arbitrage. You have 6 weeks.
choices: By feasibility-times-learning: pairs trading — data available (equity prices), signal simple (z-score), costs modelable, validation clean (cointegration tests), and it exercises statistics + time series + backtest honesty. Skew trading needs options data (harder to get clean); vol arbitrage needs intraday data and market-making realism. Pick the strategy you'll VALIDATE properly in 6 weeks — a finished honest pairs backtest beats an unfinished vol-arb dream.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The selection criteria: data availability, validatability in the time budget, and coverage of the ladder's skills. Pairs hits statistics (cointegration), time series (half-life), and the full honesty protocol — maximum learning per week. 'Most impressive' optimizes for the interviewer's first impression; 'finishable and honest' optimizes for the interview's deep questions, which is where offers are decided.
scenarios.hint: What maximizes learning per week under the deadline?
evidence: One strategy, fully validated. Depth beats breadth.

scenarios.title: The Dirty Quotes
scenarios.situation: Your option-chain download has quotes violating arbitrage bounds (calls below intrinsic). Your surface builder crashes.
choices: Clean AND document: filter arb-violating quotes (log every removal with reason), make the inverter bounds-check and flag rather than crash, and write up the violations found — stale quotes, wide spreads, bad prints. The write-up is a feature: it proves market literacy. Never silently drop data; never crash on it. The data layer's job is to be honest about dirt.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The three options map to three failures: silent deletion (unreproducible), using garbage (poisoned surface), abandoning real data (never learning market dirt). The professional standard: filter with a logged reason, validate inputs at every boundary, document the dirt found. Real market data is always dirty — handling it visibly is the skill. The violations write-up becomes a capstone highlight.
scenarios.hint: What does each alternative sacrifice?
evidence: Filter with reasons, validate boundaries, document violations.

scenarios.title: The Red Test
scenarios.situation: Your binomial tree test fails: n=1000 gives 10.62 vs BS 10.4506. The tree 'mostly works.'
choices: Debug, don't ship: 10.62 vs 10.45 is 1.6% off — 'mostly works' is broken. Check u/d parameterization (u=e^{σ√Δt}?), the risk-neutral p, discounting per step, and convergence monotonicity. The test caught a real bug (probably the p or the dt scaling); fixing it teaches the tree's mechanics. A red test is the system working — shipping past it is the failure.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The tolerance-loosening temptation is the test-suite death spiral: each loosening hides the next bug. 1.6% on a vanilla is enormous (it's the whole edge in most trades). The likely culprits: p using the wrong rate, dt mis-scaled, or u/d not matching σ. The debugging IS the learning — the tree's parameterization is exactly what interviews probe. Green tests are the credibility; earn them.
scenarios.hint: What does loosening the tolerance cost?
evidence: Red tests are the system working
Debug the 1.6%. Loosening hides the next bug.

scenarios.title: The Honest Number
scenarios.situation: Your walk-forward backtest shows gross Sharpe 1.4, net-of-costs 0.7. The one-pager goes to an interviewer.
choices: Net 0.7, first and bold: the honest number leads because the interviewer's first question will be 'net of costs?' — leading with it proves you asked it yourself. Then show the gross-to-net bridge (turnover × cost model) as the analysis. A candidate who volunteers the haircut is trusted; one who hides it is audited. The 0.7 with full attribution beats a mysterious 1.4.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The signaling logic: every experienced quant discounts gross Sharpes automatically — showing net first skips their discounting and lands as honesty. The gross-to-net bridge is itself analytical content (it shows you modeled turnover and costs). The candidates who get offers are the ones whose numbers survive the interviewer's audit — lead with the survivor.
scenarios.hint: What does the interviewer do to a gross Sharpe?
evidence: The honest number first. The bridge is the analysis.

scenarios.title: The Expanding Scope
scenarios.situation: Week 4: you're tempted to add a second strategy and a live-trading connector. The core backtest isn't validated yet.
choices: Start over with a bigger plan.

Finish the core: the capstone's value is ONE validated strategy, not two half-built ones — scope creep trades depth for breadth exactly when depth is being graded. Park the ideas in a 'future work' section (shows vision without costing validation). The discipline: the checklist defines done; new ideas wait for green checks. Interviewers probe depth; half-built breadth collapses under questions.
Add the connector; live trading impresses.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The 'future work' section is the scope-management tool: it captures the ambition (interviewers like vision) without spending the validation budget. The failure mode is real: every added feature splits testing/validation time, and the interview exposes the thinnest part. Done means validated — the checklist, not enthusiasm, defines it.
scenarios.hint: What defines 'done' for the capstone?
evidence: Park new ideas in 'future work.' Depth is graded.

domains.name: Probability Foundations
domains.description: Axioms, conditional probability, Bayes, random variables, expectation, and the distributions quants use daily.

scenarios.title: The Three Doors
scenarios.situation: You're on a game show: three doors, one prize. You pick door 1. The host (who knows) opens door 3, revealing no prize. Should you switch to door 2?
choices: Switch, but only 50/50 — the host might be tricking you.

Switch: your door had 1/3 initially; the host's action concentrates the remaining 2/3 on door 2. The host's knowledge is information — opening door 3 wasn't random, it was constrained (never the prize, never your door). P(prize|switch) = 2/3.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The key: the host's choice is INFORMED — he avoids the prize deliberately, so 'door 3 empty' carries information about door 2. Bayes: P(prize behind 2 | host opens 3) = 2/3. The 50/50 intuition treats the host's action as random; it isn't. (If the host opened randomly and happened to reveal no prize, THEN it'd be 50/50 — the information structure decides.)
scenarios.hint: Was the host's door choice random or informed?
evidence: Host's informed action concentrates 2/3 on the other door. Switch.

scenarios.title: The Shared Birthday
scenarios.situation: How many people for a 50% chance that two share a birthday? Most guess ~183.
scenarios.prompt: What is the answer, and why is intuition wrong?
choices: 23: compute via the complement (all birthdays distinct) — P = 1 - (365/365)(364/365)...(343/365) ≈ 0.507. Intuition counts pairs against 365 (linear thinking); the answer counts PAIRS (23 choose 2 = 253 comparisons — quadratic). The pairs, not the people, drive it.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The complement calculation: with 23 people there are C(23,2)=253 pairs, each with 1/365 match chance — 253/365 ≈ 0.69 expected matches, giving ~50% at-least-one probability. Intuition fails because it thinks '23 people vs 365 days' (linear) instead of '253 pairs vs 365 days' (quadratic). The general lesson: count the comparisons, not the items.
scenarios.hint: How many pairs are there among 23 people?
evidence: 23 people, 253 pairs. Count comparisons, not items.

scenarios.title: The Gambler's Fallacy
scenarios.situation: A roulette wheel shows 8 reds in a row. A gambler bets big on black: 'it's due.' The casino welcomes him.
scenarios.prompt: Why is he wrong (assuming a fair wheel)?
choices: Independence: each spin is independent — P(black) = 18/37 regardless of history. 'Due' confuses the law of large numbers (long-run frequencies converge) with short-run compensation (the wheel has no memory). The 8 reds are evidence of nothing about spin 9.
8 reds prove the wheel is biased.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Independence means history doesn't change the odds — the wheel has no memory. The law of large numbers says the PROPORTION converges as n→∞; it doesn't say the wheel 'corrects' (the 8 reds get diluted, not compensated). The subtle point: 8 reds IS evidence the wheel might be biased (that's a different, Bayesian question) — but 'due' as compensation is the fallacy.
scenarios.hint: Does the wheel remember spin 8 when spinning spin 9?
evidence: History doesn't change odds. LLN dilutes; it doesn't compensate.

scenarios.title: The Positive Test
scenarios.situation: A test is 99% accurate (sensitivity = specificity = 99%). You test positive for a disease with 0.1% prevalence. What's P(disease|+)?
choices: ~9%: P(D|+) = 0.99×0.001 / (0.99×0.001 + 0.01×0.999) = 0.00099/0.01098 ≈ 0.090. The 99% accuracy feels decisive; the 0.1% prior dominates — most positives are false (1% of the 99.9% healthy = 0.999% vs 0.099% true). Base rates dominate rare-event testing.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The arithmetic: numerator 0.99×0.001=0.00099; denominator adds false positives 0.01×0.999=0.00999; total 0.01098; ratio ≈ 0.0902. The '99% accurate' intuition commits the base-rate fallacy — accuracy is P(+|D), but you need P(D|+), and the prior (0.1%) does the heavy lifting. Verify: 0.00099/0.01098 = 0.09016... ≈ 9%. Correct.
scenarios.hint: Which is bigger: true positives or false positives?
evidence: P(D|+)≈9% here. Accuracy ≠ posterior. Compute the denominator.

scenarios.title: The St. Petersburg Game
scenarios.situation: A coin is flipped until heads: win $2^k if heads on flip k. Expected value = infinite (sum 2^k × 2^-k = sum 1). How much would you pay to play?
choices: Diminishing marginal utility (Bernoulli): utility of money is concave (log), so E[utility] is finite — you'd pay ~$2-4. Alternatively: finite bankrolls cap the payout, or risk aversion. The paradox shows EV alone doesn't determine rational price — utility and constraints matter. Expected value isn't expected happiness.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The EV really is infinite (each term = 1, infinite terms) — the math is right, the decision rule is wrong. Bernoulli's resolution: maximize expected UTILITY with concave u (log), giving finite value. Modern takes: finite bankrolls truncate the series; Kelly sizing; ergodicity (time-average vs ensemble-average). The interview lesson: EV is the start of decision theory, not the end.
scenarios.hint: Is the paradox in the math or the decision rule?
evidence: Infinite EV, finite utility. Concave u (log) → pay ~$2-4.

scenarios.title: The Boy-or-Girl Paradox
scenarios.situation: 'A family has two children; at least one is a boy. What's P(both are boys)?' Most say 1/2.
scenarios.prompt: What is it, and what variant gives 1/2?
choices: 1/3: the sample space given 'at least one boy' is {BB, BG, GB} — 3 equally likely, 1 favorable. The 1/2 variant: 'a SPECIFIC child (the elder) is a boy' → {BB, BG} → 1/2. The information structure ('at least one' vs 'this one') changes the conditioning set — precision about what's given decides.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. 'At least one boy' eliminates only GG, leaving 3 outcomes; 'the elder is a boy' eliminates GB and GG, leaving 2. Same family, different information, different answer — the conditioning event is everything. This is the interview's precision test: state the sample space explicitly, or the paradox owns you.
scenarios.hint: What exactly was conditioned on?
evidence: 'At least one' → 1/3. 'This one' → 1/2. The given decides.

scenarios.title: The Tower in Action
scenarios.situation: You need E[X] but X depends on a hidden regime Y (bull/bear). You can compute E[X|Y=bull] and E[X|Y=bear] and P(Y).
choices: Tower property: E[X] = E[E[X|Y]] = E[X|bull]P(bull) + E[X|bear]P(bear). Condition on what you can compute, then uncondition by averaging over the conditioning variable. This pattern — condition, compute, collapse — appears in every pricing derivation.
E[X] is unknowable with hidden regimes.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The tower property (law of total expectation) is the formal 'compute via cases': E[E[X|Y]] = E[X]. Note the weights are P(Y) — 'average the two' only works for 50/50. In pricing, Y is often the path/event you condition on (binomial tree!), and the tower collapses the tree to the price. It's the most-used theorem you can name.
scenarios.hint: What weights the conditional expectations?
evidence: Condition, compute, collapse. Weights are P(Y).

domains.name: Statistics & Inference
domains.description: Estimation, hypothesis testing, regression, and the limits of inference — the statistics quants actually use.

scenarios.title: The 20 Strategies
scenarios.situation: A quant tests 20 strategy variants. One has p = 0.03. She presents it as 'statistically significant.'
choices: Multiple testing: at alpha=0.05, testing 20 useless strategies expects 1 false positive — the 'discovery' is the expected noise. Fix: Bonferroni (require p < 0.05/20 = 0.0025), FDR control, or pre-registered out-of-sample validation. The presented p-value is unadjusted for the search.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The p-value's meaning assumes ONE pre-specified test; 20 tests make 0.03 unsurprising under the null. This is strategy-mining, the quant p-hacking: the reported significance ignores the search that found it. Bonferroni is conservative; FDR (Benjamini-Hochberg) is the modern standard; out-of-sample is the gold standard. Always ask: 'how many did you test?'
scenarios.hint: How many tests were run, and what does chance alone produce?
evidence: 20 tests at 0.05 → 1 false positive expected. Correct or validate OOS.

scenarios.title: The Undetectable Edge
scenarios.situation: A strategy has true Sharpe 0.8. One year of daily data (252 obs) gives p = 0.20 — 'not significant.' The PM kills it.
choices: Underpowered test: Sharpe 0.8 needs ~4 years of daily data for 80% power at 5% significance (t = Sharpe×sqrt(T)). One year can't detect it — 'not significant' means 'insufficient data,' not 'no edge.' The PM confused absence of evidence with evidence of absence. Power analysis should precede the test.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The t-stat for Sharpe: t ≈ SR × sqrt(T_years) = 0.8 × 1 = 0.8, far below the ~2 needed for significance. The edge is real but undetectable at this n — the test was doomed before it ran. Power analysis (required n for the minimum interesting effect) should gate every test. Killing strategies for underpowered insignificance destroys real alpha.
scenarios.hint: What t-stat does Sharpe 0.8 produce in 1 year?
evidence: t ≈ SR√T. Underpowered 'insignificance' isn't absence. Size the test.

scenarios.title: The Missing Variable
scenarios.situation: A regression of returns on sentiment shows a strong coefficient. But sentiment correlates with volatility, which is omitted. The coefficient is biased.
scenarios.prompt: What is the violation, and the fix?
choices: Omitted variable bias: violating exogeneity (E[e|X]≠0) — the omitted volatility lives in the error term, correlated with sentiment, biasing its coefficient. Fix: include the confounder, or use instruments/experiments. No standard error warns you; the bias is silent. This is why 'control for confounders' is identification, not tidiness.
The coefficient is fine; R² is high.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Exogeneity is the assumption that bites: E[error|X]=0 fails when omitted variables correlate with included ones, and OLS then attributes the omitted's effect to the included. The bias direction follows the correlations. High R² doesn't save you — the model fits well and means something else. In quant, this is factor-model misspecification: the 'alpha' is just omitted beta.
scenarios.hint: Where did the omitted variable go, and what does it correlate with?
evidence: Correlated omissions live in the error, biasing coefficients silently.

scenarios.title: Two Philosophies
scenarios.situation: A Bayesian reports P(theta > 0 | data) = 0.93. A frequentist reports p = 0.04. A PM asks: 'so what's the probability the strategy works?'
choices: Give the Bayesian number with its prior stated: 0.93 IS P(works|data) — the PM's question, answered, conditional on the prior. The p-value answers a different question (P(data|H0)) and the PM's inversion ('p=0.04 so 96% it works') is the inverse fallacy. Report the posterior, name the prior, show sensitivity.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The PM asked the Bayesian question (probability the strategy works given data) — only the posterior answers it. The p-value's common misreading as P(H0 false) is the inverse fallacy. The honest answer: 0.93 under the stated prior, here's how it moves with other priors. Two frameworks, two questions — match the answer to the question asked.
scenarios.hint: Which number answers the PM's actual question?
evidence: P(works|data) is Bayesian. p-values don't invert. State the prior.

scenarios.title: The 500 Factors
scenarios.situation: A model has 500 factors, 1000 observations. In-sample R² = 0.95. Out-of-sample R² = -0.3 (worse than the mean).
choices: Overfitting: p/n = 0.5 — the model memorized noise. Negative OOS R² means worse than predicting the mean. Fix: regularization (ridge/lasso with CV), dimensionality reduction, or fewer factors — trading in-sample fit for out-of-sample validity. The bias-variance trade made visible: 500 factors bought variance, not signal.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D (index 3). With 500 factors and 1000 points, OLS fits noise — R²=0.95 is memorization, and OOS -0.3 proves it (worse than the naive mean!). Regularization (penalized regression, CV-tuned) constrains the fit; the honest metric is always out-of-sample. 'More data' helps but doesn't fix the methodology; the methodology must change.
scenarios.hint: What does negative out-of-sample R² mean?
evidence: p≈n/2 memorizes noise. Penalize, CV-tune, validate OOS.

scenarios.title: The Survivors' Fund
scenarios.situation: A study of mutual fund performance uses current funds only. Average alpha looks positive. The researcher concludes active management works.
choices: Survivorship bias: dead funds (the failures) are excluded — only survivors remain, inflating the average. The sample is conditioned on survival, which correlates with performance. Fix: point-in-time universes including defunct funds. The 'positive alpha' is selection, not skill.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Conditioning on survival selects for luck+skill, and the average over survivors overstates the population. This is everywhere in finance: backtests on current index members, 'successful trader' interviews, fund databases without dead funds. The fix is the point-in-time universe — what existed THEN, including what later died. Survivorship bias flatters every selected sample.
scenarios.hint: Who's missing from the sample?

scenarios.title: Interval vs p-value
scenarios.situation: Two reports land on your desk: (a) 'effect significant, p = 0.04'; (b) 'effect = 0.5% ± 2.0% (95% CI)'.
scenarios.prompt: Which is more informative for a trading decision, and why?
choices: (b): the CI shows magnitude AND uncertainty — 0.5% ± 2.0% includes zero and economically negligible values; the 'significance' in (a) hides that the effect is tiny and uncertain. p-values collapse everything into a threshold; intervals preserve the information. For decisions (trade? invest?), (b) is actionable, (a) is a riddle.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The CI reveals what the p-value hides: the effect could be zero, could be negative, and is small regardless. 'Significant' at p=0.04 with a wide CI is statistical significance without practical significance — the distinction that matters for capital. Report intervals; the p-value is the footnote, not the headline.
scenarios.hint: Is the effect economically meaningful, or just 'significant'?
evidence: Magnitude + uncertainty beats threshold. Report CIs.

domains.name: Stochastic Processes
domains.description: Random walks, Brownian motion, martingales, Itô calculus, and geometric Brownian motion — the machinery of derivatives.

scenarios.title: The sqrt(dt) Rule
scenarios.situation: A junior simulates Brownian motion with increments N(0, dt) — standard deviation dt, not sqrt(dt). The paths look 'too smooth.'
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong, and what is the correct scaling?
choices: Variance must scale linearly with time: Var(W_t) = t requires per-step variance dt, hence sd = sqrt(dt). With sd = dt, total variance after N steps is N·dt² = T·dt → 0 as dt→0 — the paths collapse to zero. The sqrt is what keeps volatility alive in the continuous limit. Always: sd = sigma·sqrt(dt).
dt is fine; the junior needs more steps.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The scaling argument: N steps of variance v give total variance Nv; we need Nv = T, with N = T/dt, so v = dt and sd = sqrt(dt). With sd = dt: total var = T·dt → 0 — degenerate. This is THE discretization rule for all SDEs: diffusion terms scale with sqrt(dt), drift with dt. Get it backwards and every simulation is wrong.
scenarios.hint: What is the total variance after N steps with sd = dt?
evidence: Variance linear in time. Diffusion √dt, drift dt.

scenarios.title: The Discounted Price
scenarios.situation: A junior notes that under the real-world measure, the discounted stock price drifts — so it can't be a martingale there.
scenarios.prompt: Under which measure is the discounted stock price a martingale, and why does it matter?
choices: Under Q (risk-neutral): E_Q[e^{-rT}S_T] = S_0. It matters because it's the no-arbitrage condition in probability language — and it means option prices are discounted Q-expectations of payoffs. Under P, the discounted price drifts (by mu - r); only Q makes it a martingale.
Under P — real probabilities price options.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The martingale property under Q IS the fundamental theorem of asset pricing (first FTAP): no arbitrage ⟺ existence of Q making discounted prices martingales. Pricing = discounted Q-expectation follows directly. Under P the discounted stock has drift (mu - r) — it's not a martingale, and P-expectations don't give arbitrage-free prices.
scenarios.hint: What does the martingale property give you for pricing?
evidence: Discounted prices are Q-martingales. Pricing = discounted Q-expectation.

scenarios.title: The Missing Half
scenarios.situation: A student applies the ordinary chain rule to f(W_t) = W_t², getting df = 2W dW. The expectation is wrong.
choices: The Itô correction: df = 2W dW + dt (since f'' = 2, the ½σ²f_xx term with σ=1 gives ½·2·dt = dt). Taking expectations: E[W_t²] = t, not 0 — the ordinary chain rule loses the dt term, which is exactly the variance accumulation. (dW)² = dt is the rule ordinary calculus lacks.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Itô's lemma: df = f' dW + ½f'' dt. For f = W²: 2W dW + dt. The dt term integrates to t, giving E[W_t²] = t — the known variance. The ordinary chain rule drops it because ordinary calculus assumes (dx)² = 0; Brownian motion has (dW)² = dt (quadratic variation). This single correction generates the entire BS PDE.
scenarios.hint: What is E[W_t²], and which term produces it?

scenarios.title: Mean vs Median
scenarios.situation: A stock has 8% expected return, 30% vol. An investor holds 10 years. What does she TYPICALLY get vs the EXPECTED value?
choices: Expected: 100·e^{0.08×10} = 100·e^0.8 ≈ $222.55. Typical (median): 100·e^{(0.08-0.045)×10} = 100·e^0.35 ≈ $141.91. The median lags by σ²/2 = 4.5%/year — volatility drag. Most paths underperform the mean; the mean is pulled up by rare huge outcomes. 'Expected return' misleads about typical experience.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The Itô correction strikes: median growth = mu - σ²/2 = 0.08 - 0.045 = 0.035. Check: e^0.8 = 2.2255 → $222.55; e^0.35 = 1.4191 → $141.91. The gap (volatility drag) is why leveraged ETFs decay and why 'expected return' overstates typical wealth. For lognormal, always distinguish mean from median.
scenarios.hint: Which grows at mu, and which at mu - σ²/2?
evidence: Median lags mean by σ²/2. Typical ≠ expected.

scenarios.title: Rates Don't GBM
scenarios.situation: A junior models interest rates with GBM. Rates go negative in reality; GBM stays positive. Also, rates clearly pull back toward historical means.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right model class, and why?
choices: Mean-reverting (OU/Vasicek/CIR): dx = κ(θ-x)dt + σdW — pulls toward θ at speed κ, allows negatives (Vasicek) or prevents them (CIR, square-root diffusion). GBM's exponential growth and positivity suit stocks, not rates. Model choice follows the empirical behavior: mean reversion is the stylized fact for rates.
GBM with a floor at zero.
Rates are unpredictable; don't model them.
GBM is fine; the junior is right.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The stylized facts decide: rates mean-revert (central bank policy, economic cycles) and can go negative (Europe, Japan). OU/Vasicek captures both; CIR adds positivity via sqrt diffusion. GBM's geometric growth is wrong-shaped for rates. The general principle: match the SDE to the empirical dynamics, not to familiarity.
scenarios.hint: What do rates do that GBM can't capture?
evidence: Rates mean-revert → OU/Vasicek/CIR. GBM is for stocks.

scenarios.title: The Clever Stopping Rule
scenarios.situation: A trader claims a stop-loss/take-profit rule turns a fair game profitable: 'cut losses, let winners run.'
choices: For a martingale with bounded stopping time: E[M_τ] = E[M_0] — no stopping rule creates edge from a fair game. 'Cut losses, let winners run' changes the DISTRIBUTION (skew) but not the EXPECTATION. The trader confuses a nicer shape with a higher mean. Unbounded rules (double-until-win) fail differently: infinite capital required.
He's right; risk management creates edge.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B (index 1). Optional stopping is the formal 'you can't beat a fair game': bounded stopping preserves expectation. The stop-loss/take-profit DOES change the P&L distribution (cuts left tail, caps right) — which can match risk preferences — but E stays. The martingale betting system (double after losses) seems to win until you hit the capital constraint or table limit: unbounded stopping, infinite risk.
scenarios.hint: Does the rule change the mean or just the shape?
evidence: Bounded stopping preserves E. Shape changes; mean doesn't.

scenarios.title: The Vanishing Drift
scenarios.situation: Two quants estimate mu differently (8% vs 12%) but agree on sigma (20%). They price the same option. Do they disagree on the price?
choices: No: arbitrage-free price uses Q (drift r), and mu vanishes via Girsanov — the price depends on r, sigma, and payoff, not mu. Their mu disagreement affects forecasts and hedging P&L attribution, not the price. This is why options can be priced without agreeing on expected returns — the deepest fact in derivatives.
Yes; higher mu means higher call price.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Girsanov shifts the drift to r regardless of the P-drift: the market price of risk absorbs mu entirely. The option price is mu-free — which is why Black-Scholes needs no expected-return estimate, the hardest parameter to estimate. Their disagreement matters for delta-hedging P&L (realized vs implied) and risk, never for the arbitrage-free price.
scenarios.hint: Where did mu go?
evidence: Girsanov → drift r. Price needs sigma, not mu.

domains.name: Derivatives Pricing
domains.description: No-arbitrage, binomial trees, Black-Scholes, Greeks, and implied volatility — the pricing core.

scenarios.title: The Parity Violation
scenarios.situation: You see: C = 12.0, P = 4.0, S = 100, K = 100, r = 5%, T = 1. Parity says C - P should equal S - Ke^{-rT} = 4.877. But C - P = 8.0.
choices: Arbitrage: calls are rich vs puts by 3.12. Sell the call, buy the put, buy the stock, borrow Ke^{-rT}: cash flow today = +12 - 4 - 100 + 95.12 = +3.12, and at expiry the positions cancel exactly (the portfolio replicates zero). Lock in 3.12 risk-free. (In practice: check borrow costs, spreads, and American-exercise — textbook arb meets market friction.)
Buy the call; it's going up.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The replicating portfolio: -C + P + S - Ke^{-rT} cash has zero payoff at expiry in all states (that's the parity proof) but costs -3.12 today — negative cost for zero payoff is arbitrage. The construction generalizes: any parity violation is a machine for risk-free profit, which is why violations don't survive. Friction (spreads, borrow, American exercise) is why small 'violations' persist.
scenarios.hint: What portfolio has zero payoff at expiry but nonzero cost today?
evidence: Replicate, compare, lift the free money. Friction bounds it.

scenarios.title: The 75% That Isn't
scenarios.situation: A one-step tree prices a call with risk-neutral p = 0.75. A junior says 'the stock has a 75% chance of going up.'
choices: p is the no-arbitrage pricing weight, forced by the replication condition (p = (e^{rΔt}-d)/(u-d)) — it makes the stock's expected return r under Q. It is NOT the real-world probability (which involves mu and is unobservable from options). The junior confuses Q with P — the canonical derivatives error. Prices don't reveal real probabilities.
Nothing; p is the real probability.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The risk-neutral p is determined by u, d, r alone — no mu anywhere. It's the weight that makes discounted prices martingales, i.e., the weight consistent with no arbitrage. Real probabilities (P) need mu, which options can't identify. The deep lesson: derivatives are priced by replication, not prediction — Q is about hedging, not forecasting.
scenarios.hint: What determines p — replication or forecasting?
evidence: Forced by no-arbitrage. Prices hedge; they don't predict.

scenarios.title: Exercise the Put
scenarios.situation: An American put is deep in the money (S=50, K=100) with 1 month left. The tree says exercise value (50) exceeds hold value (48).
scenarios.prompt: Should you exercise, and why can this happen for puts but (almost) never for calls?
choices: American and European are the same.

Exercise: 50 > 48, take the intrinsic. American puts gain from early exercise because of time value of money — K received today vs later (K - Ke^{-rT} > 0). American calls on non-dividend stocks never exercise early (the call's time value + interest on K exceeds any benefit) — Merton's theorem. With dividends, calls CAN exercise optimally just before ex-div.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The economics: exercising the put early banks K now vs K later — the interest (K(1-e^{-rT})) can exceed the put's remaining time value when deep ITM. For non-dividend calls, the stock has no carry benefit to capture early and the strike payment is deferred — waiting dominates. Dividends break this: capture the dividend by exercising before ex-div. The tree's max(exercise, hold) IS this logic, node by node.
scenarios.hint: What do you gain by exercising the put early?
evidence: Time value of K. Calls (no-div): never. Dividends change it.

scenarios.title: The Gamma-Theta Trade
scenarios.situation: You're long gamma (long ATM straddle). Each day you delta-hedge. Some days you make money, some you lose.
scenarios.prompt: What determines your P&L, and what is the fair price of the trade?
choices: P&L ≈ ½ΓS²(realized² - implied²)dt per day — you profit when realized variance exceeds the implied variance you paid. The theta you bleed daily IS the implied variance cost: fair when realized = implied. Long gamma is a bet that realized vol beats implied — the trade's breakeven is the implied vol itself.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The gamma-theta relationship: theta ≈ -½ΓS²σ_implied²dt (for delta-hedged), while gamma scalping earns ½ΓS²σ_realized²dt. Net: ½ΓS²(σ_real² - σ_imp²)dt. The straddle is a pure vol bet — direction hedged away, leaving the variance spread. This is the economics of every vol trade: you're long or short the gap between realized and implied.
scenarios.hint: What are you actually betting on with a hedged straddle?

scenarios.title: Reading the Skew
scenarios.situation: Equity index puts (90% strike) trade at 28% IV; calls (110%) at 18% IV. ATM is 20%.
scenarios.prompt: What does the market fear, and how do you trade the view that it's overdone?
choices: The market overpays for downside protection — crash fear (leverage effect, gap risk). If overdone: sell the skew — e.g., risk reversal (long 110% call, short 90% put) or put-spread collars — collecting the skew premium. The risk: the skew exists because crashes happen; 'overdone' needs a catalyst view, not just a level. Skew trades are short-crash insurance — size for the crash.
Buy the puts; fear is justified.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The skew's economics: index downside is systematic (can't diversify), so protection is structurally bid — the 28 vs 18 gap prices crash risk. Selling skew = selling crash insurance: steady premium, catastrophic left tail. The trade needs an edge on crash probability, not just 'rich' — the market's fear is usually rational. Size for the state where you're wrong.
scenarios.hint: Why are downside puts structurally bid?
evidence: Downside is systematic. Selling skew = selling insurance.

scenarios.title: The IV That Isn't There
scenarios.situation: A deep OTM option's price is below the minimum BS price at any positive vol (it's worth 0.01, below intrinsic+time floor). Your inverter crashes.
choices: The price violates BS arbitrage bounds — no IV exists (bisection bracket fails). Causes: stale quote, wide spread (mid below bound), or the bound itself (American/dividends). Fix: don't invert garbage — check bounds first (C ≥ max(S-Ke^{-rT},0)), use the bid/ask appropriately, flag rather than crash. Robust inverters validate inputs.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Implied vol exists only if the price is within BS's attainable range — below the no-arb bound, no σ fits, and the solver correctly fails. The bug is inverting without validating: check C ≥ S - Ke^{-rT} (and ≥ 0) first. Real desks hit this with stale marks and wide markets — the fix is input validation and graceful flagging, not a better solver. Never let a pricer crash on market data.
scenarios.hint: Can every price be inverted to an IV?
evidence: No IV exists below arb bounds. Check, flag, don't crash.

scenarios.title: The Barrier Twist
scenarios.situation: A down-and-out call (knocked out if S hits 80) is cheaper than the vanilla call. A client asks why, and when the discount is largest.
choices: The barrier removes payoffs: paths hitting 80 die, so the option is worth less — the discount = value of the knocked-out paths. Largest when the barrier is near spot (high knock-out probability) and vol is high (more barrier hits). Price via reflection principle (closed form for single barriers) or trees/MC with barrier monitoring — mind discrete vs continuous monitoring (discrete monitoring weakens the barrier: fewer chances to knock out, so the option is worth MORE than the continuous version).
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The economics: you're selling the knock-out contingency — the client accepts the barrier risk for the discount. Pricing: the reflection principle gives closed forms for continuous single barriers; discrete monitoring (daily close) weakens the barrier (option worth MORE than continuous version). The common pitfall: pricing discrete with the continuous formula — misprices by the monitoring gap. Always match the contract's monitoring.
scenarios.hint: What exactly are you selling when you sell a barrier option?
evidence: Discount = knocked-out paths. Mind discrete vs continuous.

domains.name: Risk Management
domains.description: VaR, expected shortfall, stress testing, and the risk frameworks that keep firms alive.

scenarios.title: The $10M VaR
scenarios.situation: A desk reports 1-day 99% VaR of $10M. The CEO asks: 'so our worst loss is $10M?'
choices: VaR is a quantile, not a maximum: 1% of days exceed $10M, and VaR says nothing about by how much — the $1B loss and the $11M loss are identical to VaR. For 'how bad,' use expected shortfall (tail average). The CEO's question reveals the classic VaR misunderstanding; the risk manager's job is the correction.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The quantile definition: P(loss > VaR) = 1%. The tail beyond is unmeasured — that's exactly where crises live (2008's losses were '25-sigma' by VaR models). ES answers the CEO's real question. The correction matters because 'worst case $10M' thinking sizes capital for the quantile, not the catastrophe.
scenarios.hint: What does VaR say about the 1% beyond the threshold?
evidence: Quantile, not maximum. ES for 'how bad.'

scenarios.title: Diversification Increases Risk?
scenarios.situation: Two desks each have VaR $5M; the combined VaR is $12M. The CRO is confused: 'diversification should help.'
choices: VaR isn't subadditive: combined VaR CAN exceed the sum — the textbook coherence failure. (Example: two heavy-tailed bets that rarely coincide; separately each is usually fine, together the joint tail is worse than the sum suggests.) ES is subadditive and wouldn't do this. The CRO's confusion is justified — the metric is at fault, not diversification.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Subadditivity (VaR(A+B) ≤ VaR(A)+VaR(B)) is the coherence axiom VaR violates: with skewed/heavy-tailed risks, the combined quantile can exceed the sum. This isn't a data error — it's mathematical. It's why Basel moved to ES for capital: a risk measure that punishes diversification is dangerous. The CRO should switch metrics, not desks.
scenarios.hint: Which coherence axiom does VaR violate?
evidence: Not subadditive. ES is. Basel switched for this.

scenarios.title: Ten Breaches
scenarios.situation: A 99% VaR model shows 10 breaches in 250 days. The desk says 'bad luck.'
choices: No: expected breaches = 2.5; P(≥10 | p=0.01) is tiny (~0.0001 — compute binomial). The Kupiec test rejects decisively — the model underestimates risk (or the regime changed). 'Bad luck' at 10 vs 2.5 expected is a 4x miss; luck doesn't do that. Recalibrate or replace the model; don't trade through it.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The binomial math: P(X≥10) with n=250, p=0.01 — mean 2.5, sd ≈ 1.57; 10 is ~4.8 sd out, probability ≈ 0.0001. That's not luck, it's a broken model (or a regime the model never saw). Backtesting is VaR's falsification mechanism — the traffic-light system (green <5, yellow 5-9, red ≥10) exists precisely to overrule 'bad luck.'
scenarios.hint: What is P(≥10 breaches) if the model is right?
evidence: 10 vs 2.5 expected: reject. Traffic-light: red zone.

scenarios.title: What Kills You?
scenarios.situation: The regulator asks: 'What scenario would wipe out 50% of your capital, and how plausible is it?'
scenarios.prompt: What are they asking for, and why?
choices: Reverse stress testing: start from the firm's death and work backward to the scenarios causing it — then judge plausibility. It defeats the 'we never imagined it' defense by forcing imagination of ruin first. The plausibility judgment is the point: implausible deaths need no action; plausible ones need limits now.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Reverse stress testing inverts the usual flow: instead of scenario → loss, it's ruin → scenario. It finds the firm's specific vulnerabilities (concentrations, wrong-way risks, liquidity gaps) that forward scenarios miss. The regulatory logic: firms prepare for imagined scenarios but die from unimagined ones — so start from death. The deliverable is the kill-scenario list with plausibility assessments and mitigants.
scenarios.hint: Why start from ruin instead of from scenarios?
evidence: Ruin → scenario defeats 'never imagined it.' Then judge plausibility.

scenarios.title: The Hedge That Wasn't
scenarios.situation: A bank hedges its exposure to a counterparty with CDS... bought FROM that counterparty. The counterparty's credit worsens; the exposure grows.
scenarios.prompt: What is the risk, and why did the hedge fail?
choices: Wrong-way risk: exposure increases exactly when the counterparty's credit deteriorates — the hedge is correlated with the hedged. Buying protection from the entity you're exposed to concentrates rather than transfers risk (the CDS is worthless if they default — when you need it most). General form: any hedge whose value falls in the states where the exposure rises.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Wrong-way risk is correlation between exposure and counterparty credit quality — the hedge pays off in good states and defaults in bad ones. The AIG lesson: concentrated wrong-way exposure (CDS on subprime, sold by a subprime-exposed insurer) is systemic. The fix: diversify counterparties, collateralize, and measure the exposure-credit correlation — CVA with wrong-way adjustment.
scenarios.hint: When does the hedge pay — in good states or bad?
evidence: Exposure ↑ as credit ↓. The hedge defaults when needed.

scenarios.title: The Breached Limit
scenarios.situation: A desk breaches its VaR limit. The limit committee grants an exception 'temporarily.' Six months later the exception is permanent and the desk blows up.
choices: Limit governance: exceptions without expiry, escalation, or consequence become the new limit — the 2008 pattern (every post-mortem features ignored limits). A limit system needs: automatic escalation, time-boxed exceptions, P&L attribution of the breach, and consequences. 'Temporary' exceptions are permanent unless the process forces review.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The failure is institutional, not mathematical: limits work only if breaches have consequences. The pattern — breach, exception, normalization, blowup — recurs because exceptions are easier than de-risking. Good governance: hard stops (auto-escalate to CRO), exception half-lives (expire in days, not quarters), and breach P&L attribution (was the exception profitable or just tolerated?).
scenarios.hint: What turns a 'temporary' exception permanent?
evidence: Exceptions expire or they're the new limit. Escalate automatically.

scenarios.title: The Gap Risk
scenarios.situation: A fund's VaR looks fine, but its positions are in illiquid small-caps. In a crisis, selling moves prices 10%.
choices: Liquidity risk: VaR assumes you can exit at the mark — with illiquid positions, the act of selling IS the loss (market impact). Gap risk (overnight jumps past stops) compounds it. Fixes: liquidity-adjusted VaR (add exit-cost estimates), position-size limits vs ADV (average daily volume), and stress tests with impact. The mark is not the exit price.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. VaR's hidden assumption: frictionless exit at modeled prices. Illiquidity breaks it — the position's size relative to market depth determines the true exit cost. LTCM's lesson: the models were right about the assets, wrong about the exit. Liquidity-adjusted VaR adds the liquidation cost curve; ADV-based limits keep positions exit-able. In stress, liquidity is the risk that eats the other risks.
scenarios.hint: Can you exit at the mark?
evidence: Size vs ADV. Liquidation cost is real VaR.

domains.name: Portfolio Theory
domains.description: Markowitz, CAPM, factor models, and the portfolio construction quants live by.

scenarios.title: Below the Frontier
scenarios.situation: A client's portfolio has the same expected return as the efficient frontier portfolio but 30% more volatility.
choices: Higher vol means higher return; it's fine.

They're below the frontier — dominated: the same return is available at lower risk (or higher return at the same risk). The fix is re-optimization (or just holding the frontier portfolio). The 30% extra volatility is uncompensated risk — risk without return. Every portfolio should be ON the frontier; below it is inefficiency, pure and simple.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The frontier's definition: maximum return per unit risk. Same return + more vol = dominated — a free improvement exists. The 30% is literally uncompensated: no extra expected return for it. This is the first diagnostic of any portfolio: are you on the frontier? If not, optimize before strategizing.
scenarios.hint: Is the extra volatility compensated?
evidence: Same return + more vol = dominated. Uncompensated risk.

scenarios.title: The Error Maximizer
scenarios.situation: An optimizer puts 80% in the asset with the highest historical mean — which had one lucky year. Out-of-sample, it disappoints.
choices: Estimation error maximization: the optimizer overweights the noisiest estimates — the highest sample mean is likely the luckiest, not the best. Markowitz treats estimates as truth; the optimizer exploits their errors. Fixes: shrinkage (James-Stein, Ledoit-Wolf), constraints, Black-Litterman, or resampling. The optimizer is only as honest as its inputs.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Michaud's 'error maximizer' critique: optimization amplifies input errors — the winning asset is often the winning measurement error. Shrinkage pulls extreme estimates toward the grand mean, directly countering the mechanism. The practical rule: if the optimal portfolio looks extreme, it's probably the errors talking. Constrain, shrink, or BL.
scenarios.hint: Why did the optimizer love the luckiest asset?

scenarios.title: The Market-Neutral Book
scenarios.situation: You want a stock-picking book with zero market exposure. Your longs have beta 1.2 ($100M), shorts beta 0.9 ($100M).
scenarios.prompt: Are you market-neutral, and if not, what is the fix?
choices: No: net beta = 1.2 - 0.9 = +0.3 per $100M — $30M of market exposure remains. Fix: size shorts to 133M (1.2/0.9) for beta neutrality, or overlay index futures (short $30M beta-equivalent). Dollar-neutral ≠ beta-neutral — the distinction that blows up 'hedged' books in market moves.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Beta neutrality needs beta-weighted sizing: long beta × long $ = short beta × short $. Here 1.2×100 vs 0.9×100 — the book is net long the market by 0.3×$100M. In a -10% market, that's -$3M of 'hedged' P&L. The 2008 lesson for equity market-neutral: factor neutrality (beta, size, value) must be measured in risk units, not dollars.
scenarios.hint: Dollar-neutral or beta-neutral — which did you build?
evidence: Size by beta×$, not $. Dollar-neutral ≠ beta-neutral.

scenarios.title: Whose Alpha?
scenarios.situation: A manager shows 5% alpha vs the market. After Fama-French controls, alpha is 0.5% (insignificant).
choices: It was factor beta in disguise: the 'alpha' was exposure to size/value/momentum premia — compensated risk, not skill. The manager tilted to factors; the CAPM-only benchmark couldn't see it. True alpha is what's left after ALL known factors — and it's much rarer. This is why factor attribution precedes fee justification.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Alpha is benchmark-relative by definition — change the benchmark (add factors), change the alpha. The manager's edge was loading rewarded factors (possibly skillfully! factor timing is a skill) — but it's beta, priced risk, not idiosyncratic alpha. The fee question: factor exposure is cheap (ETFs); true alpha is dear. Attribution decides which you're buying.
scenarios.hint: Alpha relative to what?
evidence: Unexplained vs CAPM ≠ unexplained, period. Control factors first.

scenarios.title: Bet the Edge
scenarios.situation: You have a 60% win probability at even money, repeated. Kelly says bet 20%. Your PM bets 100%: 'maximize expected value.'
choices: Ruin: betting 100% — one loss wipes out (growth rate = -infinity after ruin). Kelly maximizes MEDIAN/long-run growth; full Kelly already has brutal drawdowns (~50%+); overbetting (100%) has negative growth rate despite positive EV per bet. EV per bet ≠ growth rate of capital. The PM confuses ensemble average with time average (ergodicity) — the fund dies with probability 1.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The growth rate at fraction f: g = p·ln(1+f) + q·ln(1-f); at f=1, q>0 gives ln(0) = -∞ — certain eventual ruin. Kelly (f*=0.2) maximizes g; beyond it, growth DECLINES (at f=0.4, g < g*). Positive EV with overbetting still ruins — the ergodicity lesson: what matters is the time-average growth of YOUR capital, not the ensemble average across parallel universes.
scenarios.hint: What is the growth rate at f=100%?
evidence: Overbetting ruins despite +EV. Kelly maximizes growth; half it.

scenarios.title: The 30th Stock
scenarios.situation: A portfolio has 30 stocks. Adding the 31st barely reduces volatility. The PM asks if diversification is 'done.'
choices: Idiosyncratic risk diversifies as ~1/n: going 1→30 eliminated most of it; 30→31 removes ~1/30 of the remainder — diminishing returns are the math, not a failure. What REMAINS is systematic (market) risk — undiversifiable by adding stocks. 'Done' for idiosyncratic; the remaining risk needs hedging (not more stocks) or acceptance.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Portfolio variance = systematic + idiosyncratic/n: the 1/n term dies fast (at n=30, ~3% of average idio var remains). The asymptote is systematic risk — no number of stocks removes it. The PM's intuition is right that marginal benefit collapsed; the conclusion should be 'diversification did its job' — remaining risk is managed by hedging, factor control, or sizing, not by stock #31.
scenarios.hint: What kind of risk remains at n=30?
evidence: Idiosyncratic dies as 1/n. What remains needs hedging.

scenarios.title: The Certain View
scenarios.situation: A PM has a 'certain' view: tech beats energy by 5%. He wants 100% tech. Black-Litterman with honest confidence gives 15% tilt.
choices: BL: 'certainty' about returns is never warranted — estimation error, regime change, and the market's contrary wisdom (equilibrium prior) all argue moderation. The 15% tilt IS the view, sized by its uncertainty. 100% tech is the view sized by overconfidence — the error-maximizer's portfolio. Views should move portfolios at the speed of their evidence.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Black-Litterman's confidence parameter exists precisely for this: views enter precision-weighted against the equilibrium prior. 'Certain' views ignore that the market (the prior) already priced the consensus — your edge is the deviation, and its size should reflect your information advantage honestly. Overconfident sizing is how views become blowups. The model enforces humility; the PM should listen.
scenarios.hint: How certain can a return view ever be?
evidence: Equilibrium prior + precision-weighted views. Humility by construction.

domains.name: Time Series Analysis
domains.description: Stationarity, ARMA/GARCH, cointegration, and the time-series models behind trading and risk.

scenarios.title: The Spurious Regression
scenarios.situation: Two independent random walks regress with R² = 0.7, t-stats 'significant.' The researcher claims a relationship.
choices: Spurious regression (Granger-Newbold): independent unit-root series show 'significant' relationships because both trend — the t-stats don't follow t-distributions under non-stationarity. The R² is the shared wandering, not a relationship. Fix: test for unit roots first; regress stationary transformations; or test for cointegration (the only valid levels-relationship).
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The pathology: with I(1) series, OLS t-stats diverge — 'significance' is guaranteed eventually, regardless of truth. The Durbin-Watson near 0 is the tell (residuals non-stationary). This is why 'stationarity first' is the law: difference, then regress — or find cointegration, the exception that proves the rule. Most 'amazing' levels-regressions in finance are this.
scenarios.hint: What distribution do the t-stats actually follow?
evidence: I(1) regressions lie. Difference, or prove cointegration.

scenarios.title: The Calm Before
scenarios.situation: A constant-vol VaR model says risk is low — vol has been 10% for months. Then a crisis: vol jumps to 60%, and the fund breaches VaR 15 days running.
scenarios.prompt: What failed, and what would have helped?
choices: Constant vol assumption: VaR didn't adapt — GARCH would have raised vol forecasts as shocks arrived (vol clustering), widening VaR BEFORE the worst breaches. The 15 consecutive breaches are the signature of unmodeled clustering. Fix: GARCH/EWMA vol in VaR (RiskMetrics uses λ=0.94 EWMA), so the model learns from recent shocks.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Volatility clustering means calm periods breed low VaR exactly when risk builds — then the regime flips and constant-vol VaR is blindsided daily. GARCH/EWMA adapts: each large shock raises tomorrow's vol forecast, so VaR widens into the storm. The 15-in-a-row pattern is the diagnostic — independent breaches wouldn't cluster; clustered breaches scream unmodeled dynamics.
scenarios.hint: Why did the breaches cluster?
evidence: GARCH/EWMA in VaR. Clustered breaches = unmodeled dynamics.

scenarios.title: The Broken Pair
scenarios.situation: A cointegrated pair's spread hits z = -4 (usually reverts by z = -2). The trader doubles down. The spread goes to z = -8: one company is acquired.
choices: No model-break stop: cointegration is an empirical regularity, not a law — corporate actions (M&A, bankruptcy, regime shifts) break it permanently. The spread at z=-4 was already screaming 're-test'; doubling down assumed the model. The stop-loss on the spread IS the model-risk control: when the deviation exceeds historical bounds persistently, the cointegration is suspect, not the opportunity bigger.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The meta-lesson: every statistical arbitrage has a model-break state, and the position must die when the model does. z=-4 (a ~4-sigma event under the model) is evidence AGAINST the model, not a better entry — that's the Bayesian update the trader skipped. Corporate actions are the classic breakers; re-testing cointegration and stop-losses on extreme z are the controls. Size pairs for the break, not the reversion.
scenarios.hint: Is z=-4 evidence for the trade or against the model?
evidence: Extreme z = evidence against cointegration. Re-test; stop out.

scenarios.title: The Flat Forecast
scenarios.situation: An ARMA model's 30-day forecast is a flat line at the mean. The PM calls the model 'broken.'
choices: Use the flat line as the forecast.

No — it's honest: ARMA forecasts revert to the mean at the rate of the AR roots; beyond a few lags, the unpredictable dominates and the best forecast IS the mean (with widening intervals). The flat line with growing confidence bands is the correct output. 'Broken' would be confident long-horizon point forecasts — the model knowing its limits is a feature.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The k-step ARMA forecast: the predictable component decays geometrically (φ^k), leaving the mean — the flat line is the math, not a bug. The information is in the INTERVALS (which widen to the unconditional variance). The PM wants long-horizon precision that doesn't exist; the model's refusal is its integrity. For long horizons, you need different models (structural, regime) — or humility.
scenarios.hint: What happens to the forecast intervals at long horizons?
evidence: ARMA reverts to mean. The intervals carry the information.

scenarios.title: The Leading Indicator
scenarios.situation: Variable X 'Granger-causes' Y (X's lags predict Y). The PM says 'X causes Y — let's trade on X.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the gap between Granger causality and real causality?
choices: Granger causality = predictive precedence, not causation: X helps forecast Y given the information set — but a third variable Z (driving both, X faster) produces the same pattern. True causality needs identification (experiments, instruments, structural models). Trading on Granger causality works until Z shifts — the prediction was real, the mechanism was imagined.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The classic confound: Z → X (fast) and Z → Y (slow) makes X 'Granger-cause' Y with zero causal link. The forecast CAN still trade profitably (prediction ≠ causation) — but it's fragile to Z's regime. The quant's discipline: use Granger for forecasting features, demand identification for structural claims. 'X predicts Y' is a trading signal; 'X causes Y' is a scientific claim.
scenarios.hint: What third variable produces the same pattern?
evidence: Granger = precedence. Trade the forecast; prove the cause separately.

scenarios.title: The January Effect
scenarios.situation: A strategy buys every December, sells every January — backtest Sharpe 1.2 over 40 years. The PM wants 3x leverage.
choices: Out-of-sample decay: published anomalies attenuate (McLean-Pontiff: ~50% decay post-publication) — the 40-year backtest includes the pre-discovery period when the effect was strongest. Check: post-2000 Sharpe, transaction costs (turnover!), statistical significance with data-mining correction, and whether the effect survives risk adjustment. Leveraging a decayed anomaly is how 'proven' strategies blow up.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The anomaly lifecycle: discovery → publication → arbitrage → decay. The backtest's 1.2 blends the fat early years with the thin recent ones — the tradeable Sharpe is the recent, cost-adjusted, post-publication number. Data-mining: hundreds of seasonalities were tested; the survivors are selected. Before leverage: OOS verification, cost accounting, and the humility to size the decayed edge, not the historical one.
scenarios.hint: What happens to anomalies after publication?
evidence: Post-publication attenuation. Trade the recent net Sharpe, not history.

scenarios.title: The Correlation Spike
scenarios.situation: In normal times, your assets correlate 0.3. In 2008, correlations spiked to 0.9 — diversification vanished exactly when needed.
scenarios.prompt: How should risk models handle this?
choices: Regime-conditional correlations: estimate crisis correlations separately (or use copulas with tail dependence) — single-regime models average the calm and the crisis, understating crisis risk. Risk measures should use the crisis correlation for stress/limits (conservative), normal for baseline. 'Diversification fails when needed' is the empirical fact models must encode — not assume away.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C (index 2). The stylized fact: correlations are regime-dependent, spiking in downturns (flight-to-quality, margin calls, common shocks). A single correlation matrix misstates both regimes. The fix: regime-switching models, stressed correlation inputs for VaR/stress tests, and tail-dependence-aware copulas. The risk manager's version: size positions for crisis correlations, enjoy the diversification in calm — never the reverse.
scenarios.hint: When does diversification fail?
evidence: Regime-conditional risk. Size for the crisis, not the calm.

domains.name: Monte Carlo Methods
domains.description: Simulation-based pricing, variance reduction, and the Monte Carlo techniques behind modern quant finance.

scenarios.title: The Missing Error Bar
scenarios.situation: A quant reports an exotic's price as $4.3217 from 10,000 paths. No standard error.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with the four decimals?
choices: The SE is unknown — with 10k paths and typical exotic vol, SE might be $0.05+, making digits beyond the first decimal noise. Price without SE is unquotable: the decimals imply precision the simulation doesn't have. Rule: report price ± SE; significant digits stop where the SE starts. 10k paths rarely supports 4 decimals.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The SE decides the significant digits: if SE = $0.03, the price is $4.32 ± 0.03 — the '17' is fiction. This is the most common MC reporting error: confusing computational precision (float64) with statistical precision (1/√N). Always: price ± 1.96·SE, digits to the SE's scale. The fix is either more paths, variance reduction, or fewer claimed decimals.
scenarios.hint: How many decimals does the SE support?
evidence: Price ± SE. Significant digits follow the error bar.

scenarios.title: The 100-Dimensional Option
scenarios.situation: A basket option on 100 stocks. PDE grids are impossible (100 dimensions). MC handles it easily.
scenarios.prompt: Why is MC dimension-independent, and what is the catch?
choices: MC's 1/√N error rate doesn't depend on dimension — it samples the joint distribution directly, never gridding. The catch: the CONSTANT matters — 100 correlated stocks need a 100×100 Cholesky per... (once, actually) and the payoff's variance may be huge; plus QMC's edge fades in high effective dimension. MC wins by default in high-D, but variance reduction gets harder.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The curse of dimensionality: PDE grids need n^d points; MC needs N samples regardless of d — the LLN doesn't care about dimension. The catches: (1) the constant σ in σ/√N can be large (variance reduction harder in high-D), (2) QMC degrades toward MC rates as effective dimension grows, (3) correlation structure (Cholesky) must be right. MC is the high-D default, not the high-D miracle.
scenarios.hint: What breaks for PDE grids in 100 dimensions?
evidence: 1/√N regardless of d. The constant is the catch.

scenarios.title: The Free Precision
scenarios.situation: Pricing an Asian option by MC takes 10M paths for the target SE. Using the European as a control variate, 100k paths suffice.
scenarios.prompt: Why does this work so well?
choices: Correlation: the Asian (avg-price) and European (terminal-price) payoffs on the SAME paths correlate ~0.99 — the control removes 99%+ of the variance (factor 1/(1-ρ²) ≈ 100x). The known European price (BS) anchors the adjustment. Requirements: same paths (common random numbers!), high ρ, exact E[Y]. It's 'free' because the European payoff is computed from paths you already simulated.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The variance math: Var(X - β(Y-E[Y])) = Var(X)(1-ρ²) — ρ=0.99 cuts variance 50x, ρ=0.995 cuts 100x. The same-paths requirement is crucial (common random numbers induce the correlation); independent simulations give ρ=0 and nothing. The general principle: any similar derivative with a known price is a control — baskets use indices, Americans use Europeans. Knowledge converts to precision.
scenarios.hint: What creates the correlation?
evidence: Same paths + known price. ρ→1 gives 100x fewer paths.

scenarios.title: The Exploding Weight
scenarios.situation: An importance sampler for a deep OTM option gives wild price swings across runs — sometimes 10x the true price.
choices: Weight degeneracy: the likelihood ratio explodes on some paths (tilt too aggressive or misdirected) — a few paths carry enormous weight, and the estimator's variance EXCEEDS naive MC's. The importance distribution must dominate the target where the payoff lives; a bad tilt is worse than none. Diagnose: effective sample size (ESS); fix: gentler tilt, defensive mixture (blend with the original).
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The failure mode: w = dP/dQ can be huge when Q puts little mass where P·payoff is large — the estimator becomes a lottery on rare paths. ESS = (Σw)²/Σw² near 1 means one path dominates: the estimate is fiction. The defensive mixture (α·Q_tilt + (1-α)·P) bounds the weights — robustness over optimality. Monitor ESS; it's the IS health metric.
scenarios.hint: What does ESS near 1 mean?
evidence: Bad tilt > naive variance. ESS diagnoses; defensive mixtures fix.

scenarios.title: The 1D American
scenarios.situation: A junior prices a 1D American put with Longstaff-Schwartz (100k paths, 5 minutes). The tree prices it exactly in 0.1 seconds.
choices: Match method to dimension: LSM's value is high-dimensional Americans (baskets, multi-asset) where trees explode — for 1D, trees/PDE are exact and instant.
