Using LSM in 1D pays MC noise + regression bias for nothing. The method choice IS the quant skill: trees/PDE for low-D, MC for high-D, LSM for high-D Americans. The junior used a sledgehammer to crack a nut — slowly and approximately.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The method-selection matrix: European/low-D → formulas; American/low-D → trees/PDE; exotic/high-D → MC; American/high-D → LSM. Each method has its domain; outside it, you pay (noise, bias, time) for no benefit. The junior's error isn't the code — it's the choice. Quants are paid for method selection as much as implementation.
scenarios.hint: When IS LSM the right tool?
evidence: Trees: low-D Americans. LSM: high-D Americans. Choose, don't default.

scenarios.title: The Asian's Edge
scenarios.situation: Why is Monte Carlo the natural method for Asian, barrier, and lookback options, while PDE methods struggle?
choices: Path-dependence: the payoff depends on the whole path (average, max, barrier hits) — PDE needs the path statistic as an extra state variable (dimension!), while MC just simulates paths and reads off the payoff. MC's cost is ~independent of path-dependence complexity; PDE's grows with each path feature. The structural edge: simulation speaks the payoff's language natively.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The dimensionality argument: a PDE for an Asian needs (S, A, t) — 2 spatial dimensions; a lookback needs (S, M, t); each path feature adds a dimension to the grid. MC adds ~zero cost: simulate the path, compute the running average/max along the way. This is why exotics desks are MC desks — the method matches the product's structure. Accuracy is comparable; the scaling is the story.
scenarios.hint: What does each path feature cost PDE vs MC?

scenarios.title: The Lucky Seed
scenarios.situation: A model is validated on one seed (looks great). On a different seed, it fails. The researcher reports the good seed.
scenarios.prompt: What is this, and what is the fix?
choices: Seed-picking = selection bias on randomness: the reported performance is the max over seeds, not the expectation. The fix: multiple seeds with mean ± std reported (the seed IS a hyperparameter of the evaluation), or common random numbers for comparisons (same seeds across methods — the variance reduction makes comparisons honest). A result that needs a lucky seed isn't a result.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The statistics: max over k seeds of a noisy metric overstates the true performance (selection bias, same math as p-hacking). Reporting mean ± std over seeds quantifies the Monte Carlo uncertainty of the VALIDATION itself. For method comparisons, common random numbers (same seeds) is the variance-reduced honest comparison — differences then reflect methods, not luck. Reproducibility needs the seed REPORTED, not cherry-picked.
scenarios.hint: Is the seed part of the method or the evaluation?
evidence: Mean ± std over seeds. Common random numbers for comparisons.

domains.name: Machine Learning for Quant
domains.description: Supervised learning, overfitting discipline, and ML's real (limited) role in quantitative finance.

scenarios.title: The Shuffled Backtest
scenarios.situation: A researcher runs 5-fold CV (shuffled) on 10 years of daily returns. Sharpe 2.5. Live trading: Sharpe 0.2.
choices: Lookahead via shuffling: shuffled CV trains on future data to predict the past — the model 'learns' future regimes, upcoming trends, and the test set's own future. The 2.5 is the in-sample-with-leakage number; 0.2 is reality. Fix: walk-forward/purged CV respecting time (train past → test future). Shuffled CV on time series is lookahead, full stop.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The mechanism: fold 3 trains on 2018-2020 to predict 2015 — the model sees the future (rate regimes, crises, trends) and the test isn't a test. Purged walk-forward (López de Prado) is the standard: train on [t-k, t], embargo the boundary, test [t, t+h]. The live 0.2 isn't bad luck — it's the honest number the shuffled CV concealed. Time has an arrow; CV must respect it.
scenarios.hint: What did the model see during training that it shouldn't have?

scenarios.title: The Neural Net That Lost to OLS
scenarios.situation: A deep net (10k params) gets OOS R² = 0.01 on return prediction. OLS (10 params) gets OOS R² = 0.015.
choices: The baseline rule: complexity must earn its keep — the net's 1000x parameters bought worse performance (estimation noise swamps the weak signal). In low-SNR finance, simple + regularized usually wins; the net overfits the noise OLS averages through. Always beat the linear baseline first; the burden of proof is on complexity. (The net might win with 100x data — but you don't have it.)
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The bias-variance math: with SNR ~ 0.01, the variance cost of 10k parameters dwarfs any bias advantage — the net fits noise exquisitely. OLS's 10 parameters can't overfit much. This is the finance ML prior: start simple, add complexity only with OOS evidence. 'Tune more' is usually more overfitting; the answer is less model or more (independent) data.
scenarios.hint: Why did 1000x parameters buy worse performance?
evidence: Complexity needs an OOS warrant. Low SNR favors simple.

scenarios.title: The Filing Timestamp
scenarios.situation: An NLP strategy trades on 10-K sentiment — using period-end dates. Backtest Sharpe 1.8. Point-in-time (filing dates): Sharpe 0.6.
choices: Lookahead: the market learns the 10-K at FILING (weeks after period end); period-end dating lets the model trade on information before it existed. The 1.8→0.6 collapse is the lookahead premium — the strategy's edge was time travel. Text point-in-time discipline: every document needs its AVAILABILITY timestamp (filing, wire, revision), not its content date.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The 10-K timeline: period ends Dec 31, filed late February — two months of 'knowing the future.' The backtest traded January on February's information. This is the text-data version of survivorship/lookahead bias, and it's the #1 NLP backtest bug. The fix is mechanical: join every text signal to its availability timestamp. The surviving 0.6 might be real — or the next bias; audit continues.
scenarios.hint: When did the market actually learn the 10-K's contents?
evidence: File date, not period end. Text lookahead is the #1 NLP bug.

scenarios.title: The Simulator's Apprentice
scenarios.situation: An RL execution agent crushes the simulator (saves 5bp vs TWAP). Live: it loses 2bp vs TWAP — other algos front-run its predictable schedule.
scenarios.prompt: What is the sim-to-real gap here?
choices: Adversarial response: the simulator's market is passive; real markets contain other agents that DETECT and EXPLOIT predictable patterns (the RL's learned schedule is deterministic-ish). The simulator missed the game-theoretic layer. Fixes: adversarial training (opponent agents in sim), randomization (mixed strategies), guardrails (participation caps), and online adaptation. RL optimizes the sim; the market isn't the sim.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The gap's nature: simulators model market IMPACT (your trades move prices) but rarely market RESPONSE (others adapt to your pattern). The RL learned the simulator's fixed dynamics perfectly — and the real market's adaptive dynamics punished the learned determinism. This generalizes: any ML trained in a non-adversarial sim degrades against adaptive opponents. Randomization and adversarial training are the bridges.
scenarios.hint: What did the simulator leave out?
evidence: Sims miss adversarial response. Randomize, bound, adapt online.

scenarios.title: The 50 Factors
scenarios.situation: A model uses 50 factors; feature importance says all 50 'matter.' The PM wants to monitor all 50.
scenarios.prompt: Why is the importance lying, and what should the PM monitor?
choices: Correlated features split importance: 10 correlated momentum variants each get 1/10th credit — all 'matter' a little, none decisively. Train-set importance also reflects fitting noise. Honest version: permutation importance on the TEST set, grouped by theme (momentum-as-one), plus ablation (drop the theme, measure OOS loss). The PM should monitor the 3-5 themes that survive ablation — the rest are passengers.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The splitting mechanism: importance is divided among correlated features, so redundancy looks like broad dependence. Test-set permutation is honest (it measures what the model USES on unseen data); grouping by theme answers the PM's real question ('does momentum matter?' not 'does variant #7 matter?'). Ablation is the gold standard: remove it, re-evaluate OOS. Monitor themes, not features.
scenarios.hint: What does train-set importance actually measure?
evidence: Correlated features split credit. Test-set permutation + ablation.

scenarios.title: The 3.0 Sharpe Pitch
scenarios.situation: A vendor pitches an ML strategy: backtest Sharpe 3.0, 'AI-powered.' No costs, no OOS, shuffled CV.
scenarios.prompt: Apply the audit. What is the verdict?
choices: Fails checks #1-4 at least: shuffled CV (lookahead), no costs (gross Sharpe ~ halves net with turnover), no OOS (the only metric), no baseline (probably loses to OLS). The 3.0 is a composite of self-deceptions — each fix multiplies down. Verdict: pass until walk-forward net-of-costs OOS with a beaten baseline. 'AI-powered' is marketing; the audit is due diligence.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The audit's multiplicative logic: lookahead inflates (maybe 2x), costs cut (turnover-dependent, often 30-50%), OOS halves again — 3.0 → ~0.5-0.7 realistic, before the baseline check. The vendor's refusal to show OOS/costs is itself the signal: honest strategies lead with net walk-forward numbers. The six checks exist precisely for pitches like this.
scenarios.hint: What does each missing check hide?
evidence: Lookahead, costs, OOS, baseline. 3.0 gross → ~0.5 honest.

scenarios.title: Where ML Belongs
scenarios.situation: You have one ML hire for the quant team. Where do you deploy them: return prediction, execution, or risk?
choices: Execution or risk: return prediction from prices has the worst SNR and strongest non-stationarity (the hardest ML problem); execution has clean simulators and dense rewards (RL's home turf); risk/vol forecasting has better SNR and stationarity (vol clusters predictably). Deploy ML where the data regime favors it — prediction quality follows SNR and stationarity, not enthusiasm. The hire's ROI is highest where ML's strengths meet the problem's structure.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The SNR ordering: execution microstructure (high SNR, stationary-ish) > vol forecasting (clusters) > NLP signals (inefficient processing) > raw return prediction (SNR ~0.01, regime-shifting). The hire's impact follows this ordering. 'Return prediction is the money' confuses the prize with the winnability — the money is where the edge is capturable, and that's execution/risk/NLP. Match the tool to the terrain.
scenarios.hint: Rank the problems by SNR and stationarity.
evidence: Execution/risk/NLP over raw return prediction. Deploy where data favors ML.

domains.name: Quant Interview Prep
domains.description: The interview game: mental math, probability puzzles, modeling questions, and the firms' actual bars.

scenarios.title: The Dice Game
scenarios.situation: You roll a die repeatedly, accumulating the sum. You may stop anytime and take the sum in dollars. When do you stop?
choices: Stop when the accumulated sum ≥ 20: the expected gain of another roll is E[die] = 3.5, but rolling risks... precisely: with sum s, rolling gives expected s + 3.5 ONLY if you ignore that rolling a... the clean analysis: it's optimal to continue iff E[next roll] > 0 given you keep the sum regardless — since the sum never decreases, you ALWAYS roll! Wait — the standard version: you LOSE if you exceed some cap, or the roll can bust. The interview tests whether you set up the Bellman: V(s) = max(s, E[V(s+X)]). With no bust, V(s) ≥ s always → never stop. The lesson: formalize before answering.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D (index 3) — for the no-bust version: since the sum only grows, E[continuing] ≥ current sum always, so never stop (the Bellman equation V(s) = max(s, s + 3.5) = s + 3.5). BUT the interview's real versions add twists: bust caps ('stop before exceeding 100'), costs per roll, or opponent play — each changes the Bellman. The meta-lesson: the puzzle as stated has a trivial answer; the interviewer is testing whether you formalize (Bellman) rather than guess a threshold.
scenarios.hint: What is the Bellman equation here?
evidence: V(s)=max(s, E[V(s+X)]). No bust → never stop. Twists change it.

scenarios.title: The Correlation Bet
scenarios.situation: You're offered: flip two coins; win $100 if they match, lose $100 if they differ. Fair coins, independent.
scenarios.prompt: What is the EV, and what if the coins are correlated?
choices: Independent: P(match) = 0.5 (HH+TT = 0.25+0.25), EV = 0 — fair game. Correlated: P(match) = 0.5 + ρ/2-ish (for symmetric correlation ρ: P(HH)+P(TT) = 0.5(1+ρ)) — positive correlation favors the bet; the EV = 100·ρ. The interview point: correlation structures the joint distribution; the bet's value IS the correlation. (With ρ=0.5: EV = $50.)
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The joint distribution: with correlation ρ (symmetric), P(HH) = P(TT) = (1+ρ)/4, so P(match) = (1+ρ)/2, EV = 100·ρ. Independence (ρ=0) → fair. The puzzle's lesson: many 'probabilities' are really correlation assumptions — pricing correlation products (CDOs!) is this puzzle at scale. The 2008 CDO crisis was correlation mispriced.
scenarios.hint: How does P(match) depend on ρ?

scenarios.title: The Truth-Tellers
scenarios.situation: Three people: one always tells truth, one always lies, one alternates. One question to find the truth-teller.
choices: Ask about the question itself (self-reference): 'If I asked you whether you're the truth-teller, would you say yes?' — the truth-teller says yes (truthfully); the liar says yes (lying about saying no); the alternator's answer depends on phase. Better classic: ask each 'is 2+2=4?' patterns... The robust method: ask a question whose answer you know, twice, or ask 'what would the OTHER say?' The interview tests logical structure under pressure, not the specific riddle.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The self-referential structure: embedding the question inside itself forces the liar's lie to cancel (lying about a lie = truth). The general technique for knights/knaves: ask 'what would you say if I asked X?' — both types then give the TRUE answer to X (truth-teller: truth; liar: lie about their lie). The interview lesson: logic puzzles test structured reasoning — find the invariant (the double negation), don't case-bash.
scenarios.hint: What cancels the liar's lie?
evidence: Self-reference cancels lies. Structure over cases.

scenarios.title: The Quick Estimate
scenarios.situation: 'Estimate the number of gas stations in the US.' You have 60 seconds.
choices: Fermi decomposition: population (330M) → households/drivers (~250M drivers) → miles per driver per year (~12k) → gallons per mile (~1/25) → gallons per year (~120B) → gallons per station per day (~4000?) → stations ≈ 120B/(4000×365) ≈ 82k. (Actual ~115k — order-of-magnitude right.) The grade: decomposition (break into estimable pieces), reasonable assumptions (stated!), arithmetic, sanity check. The number matters less than the structure.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The Fermi method: chain of small estimates, each stated and roughly right — errors partially cancel (some high, some low). The interview grades: (1) decomposition into knowns, (2) explicit assumptions, (3) clean arithmetic, (4) sanity check ('does 82k feel right? actual 115k — close'). Memorized answers fail the 'show your work' requirement; the structure IS the answer. Finance-flavored: 'estimate daily SPX option volume' works the same way.
scenarios.hint: What is being graded — the number or the structure?
evidence: Chain small estimates. Structure graded, number approximate.

scenarios.title: The Heated Coin
scenarios.situation: 'How would you test if a coin is biased?' The interviewer wants the statistical design, not just 'flip it.'
choices: Power analysis first: to detect bias δ at 95% confidence needs n ≈ (1.96/δ)² flips (δ=0.01 → ~38k flips!). Then: sequential testing (SPRT — stop early when significant), the null (fair), the test (binomial/z), and the practical answer ('for δ=1%, 40k flips — probably not worth it; for δ=10%, 400 flips'). The interview tests whether you think about DETECTABILITY, not just testing. Most real biases are undetectable at feasible n — that's the insight.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The power calculation: SE of p̂ = √(0.25/n); detecting δ needs δ > 1.96·SE → n > (0.98/δ)² ≈ (1/δ)². For δ=0.01: ~10k-40k flips (depending on power target). The practical punchline: small biases need enormous samples — 'is it biased 51/49?' is nearly unanswerable by flipping. This is the statistical maturity check: the question isn't 'how to test' but 'what can testing even detect.' SPRT (sequential) is the efficiency bonus.
scenarios.hint: How many flips to detect 51/49 bias?
evidence: n ≈ (1/δ)². Small biases need enormous n. Design for detectability.

scenarios.title: The Bidding Game
scenarios.situation: You and a competitor bid for a jar of coins (common value, unknown). Winner pays their bid. How should you bid?
scenarios.prompt: What is the trap, and the correct shading?
choices: Winner's curse: winning means you overestimated (the winner is the most optimistic bidder) — E[value | you win] < E[value]. Correct: shade the bid below your estimate by the adverse-selection discount (bid E[value | your signal was the HIGHEST]). Naive bidding (bid your estimate) loses money on average. The auction insight: condition on winning, not just on your signal.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The adverse selection: P(you win | value = v) is higher when your signal overstates v — winning is BAD NEWS about the value. The rational bid: E[V | signal_i, signal_i = max] — condition on the event of winning. Shading increases with bidder count and signal noise. This is the common-value auction lesson (oil leases, takeovers) — and the trading analogy: filled limit orders are adversely selected (the market traded with you for a reason).
scenarios.hint: Is winning good news or bad news about the value?
evidence: Winning = you were most optimistic. Shade for adverse selection.

scenarios.title: The Market View
scenarios.situation: Final round: 'What's interesting in markets right now?'
scenarios.prompt: What makes a good answer vs a bad one?
choices: Good: specific + reasoned — 'X is interesting because [thesis], the evidence is [data], the risk is [what breaks it], I'd express it via [trade].' Shows engagement, structure, and humility. Bad: vague ('markets are volatile'), memorized headlines, or no view ('I don't follow markets' — fatal). The bar isn't correctness (they know it's a guess) — it's whether you THINK like a market participant: thesis, evidence, risk, expression.
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. The question tests the participant's mindset: quants live in markets, and curiosity about them is a job requirement. The structure (thesis → evidence → risk → expression) mirrors real investment thinking — it's a microcosm of the job. 'Interesting' beats 'right': a well-reasoned wrong view shows the process; a correct-by-luck prediction shows nothing. Prepare one view deeply rather than five shallowly.
scenarios.hint: What is actually being tested?
evidence: Think like a participant. One deep view beats five headlines.

domains.name: Mock Assessment
domains.description: A full-length simulated quant finance assessment: timed probability, derivatives pricing, statistics, and brainteasers under interview conditions.

lessons.title: Quantitative Finance: The Ladder — Core concepts
concepts: The ladder has three rungs: (1) undergraduate preparation — multivariable calculus, linear algebra, probability and statistics at depth, programming; (2) a graduate finance credential — graduate-level finance, accounting, mathematical methods, derivatives — verified by proctored examination; (3) research-level mathematics and interview craft — stochastic calculus, case interviews, and the career fork.

The prerequisite audit is the highest-ROI study activity: list every mathematical topic quant interviews assume (conditional expectation, Bayes, distributions, linear algebra, calculus), rate yourself honestly on each, and attack the weakest first. Interview puzzles are applications of this foundation, not a separate subject.

Probability at depth means conditional reasoning: E[X | information] is the object you actually compute in interviews, trading, and research. Optimal stopping, Bayes' rule, and the law of total expectation are the three moves that solve most interview problems.

Programming for quant means vectorized numerical computing (NumPy/pandas), point-in-time-correct backtests with no look-ahead bias, and enough software engineering to make research reproducible. Speed of iteration beats speed of execution at the research stage.

A MicroMasters-style credential bundles graduate courses with a proctored comprehensive exam; its two values are the employer signal (verified graduate-level work) and the degree pathway (advanced standing toward a master's). Both values require completing the verified track.

The career fork: desk quant (derivatives pricing, hedging, trader-facing, intraday pressure), quantitative researcher (alpha research, statistical rigor, slow feedback, high idea mortality), consultant (breadth, communication, business judgment). Choose on daily-work fit; switching costs compound with seniority.

example.code:
import numpy as np

def gbm_paths(S0, mu, sigma, T, steps, n_paths, seed=0):
    # Vectorized geometric Brownian motion: the quant research workhorse
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    dt = T / steps
    Z = rng.standard_normal((n_paths, steps))
    # Exact discretization: log returns are normal with mean (mu - .5 s^2) dt
    log_rets = (mu - 0.5 * sigma ** 2) * dt + sigma * np.sqrt(dt) * Z
    S = S0 * np.exp(np.cumsum(log_rets, axis=1))
    return np.column_stack([np.full(n_paths, S0), S])

paths = gbm_paths(100, 0.05, 0.2, 1.0, 252, 100_000)
print(f"E[S_T] ~ {paths[:, -1].mean():.2f}  (theory: {100*np.exp(0.05):.2f})")
example.walkthrough: One vectorized call simulates 100,000 paths — this is the research-velocity pattern from the backtest scenario: array operations replace the 40-minute loop. The exact log-normal discretization avoids discretization bias, and comparing the simulated E[S_T] against the closed form 100·e^0.05 validates the simulation before you trust it for pricing.

pitfalls: Common trap: grinding puzzles before the audit. Every interview question is applied probability and linear algebra — without the foundation, puzzle practice has no surface to stick to.
Common trap: treating the credential as the goal. The MicroMasters-style pathway is a signal and a degree option; the underlying graduate finance knowledge is what interviews actually test.
Common trap: backtesting with look-ahead bias. If your simulation uses any information not available at the decision time, the result is fiction — point-in-time correctness comes before speed.
Common trap: choosing the fork on prestige. Desk quant, researcher, and consultant optimize different daily realities; pick the work content you'll still enjoy on a bad Tuesday.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Quant Finance Ladder move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence
lessons.try_it: Pick any process in this course. Write out the full journey from trigger to outcome, naming every system touched.

lessons.title: Anatomy of Quantitative Finance: The Ladder
concepts: Quantitative Finance: The Ladder is a multi-step process within Quantitative Finance: The Ladder: trace the full sequence from initiation to completion
See it as a journey: identify the trigger, follow each handoff, watch state change at every step
Every step depends on the previous — a failure at any point breaks the chain. Map these dependencies
Connect Quantitative Finance: The Ladder to the broader Quantitative Finance: The Ladder ecosystem — nothing operates in isolation

Step 2: Processing

pitfalls: Treating Quantitative Finance: The Ladder as an isolated component instead of part of a living flow
Skipping the dependency mapping — not asking 'what does this step need from the previous?'
Memorizing the steps without understanding WHY each one exists

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: This bootcamp is a ladder: 15 domains from probability foundations to interview prep. Work them in order — each rung assumes the previous. The domain list is the curriculum; the lessons are the lectures.

Each lesson has the same anatomy: concepts (the ideas), an example (worked, with code), pitfalls (the classic errors), and a try-it (your action). Read actively: cover the example's output and predict it before looking.
Scenarios are the exam simulator: each poses a decision, four choices, and a defensible best answer. Do them closed-book first, then read the 'why' — the explanation is the real lesson.

Labs are the workshop: implementation exercises with verifiable checks. The checks are your tests — a lab isn't done until the checks pass. Code every lab; reading about Monte Carlo isn't doing Monte Carlo.

example.code:
A study session:
  1. Read one lesson (20 min) — predict the example output first
  2. Do its domain's scenarios closed-book (30 min)
  3. Read every 'why,' especially for ones you got right by luck
  4. Implement the lab (60-90 min) until checks pass
  One domain per week = 15 weeks. The ladder rewards steady climbing.
example.walkthrough: The session structure is deliberate: prediction before reading (active recall), closed-book scenarios (retrieval practice), labs to completion (procedural fluency). Passive re-reading feels productive and isn't — the structure forces the productive kind.

pitfalls: Skipping around. The ladder is ordered; rungs assume prior rungs.
Reading scenarios' answers first. Closed-book or it doesn't count.
Half-done labs. Checks passing is the definition of done.
lessons.try_it: Do the orientation scenarios below closed-book; read every 'why.'

lessons.title: Study Strategy: The Quant's Method
concepts: Spaced repetition for formulas: Black-Scholes, Bayes, Itô's lemma, tower property — flashcards, daily. Fluency means writing them from memory, correctly, fast.
Derivation practice: re-derive key results weekly (binomial price, BS PDE sketch, CAPM). The derivation is the understanding; the formula is the souvenir.
Mental math drills: 15 minutes daily (from the interview-prep domain). Speed is trained, not gifted — log your times and watch them fall.
The error log: every mistake goes in a ledger with the concept, the correction, and a re-test date. The log is the highest-ROI study tool — it converts errors into curriculum.

example.code:
Weekly template:
  Mon-Fri: 1 lesson + scenarios (45 min) + 15 min mental math
  Sat: lab to completion (2 hrs) + error-log review
  Sun: re-derive 2 key results from memory + flashcard sweep
  Monthly: full mock assessment under timed conditions
  Consistency beats intensity. 45 minutes daily beats 8 hours Sunday.
example.walkthrough: The template's power is its sustainability: 45 minutes daily is a habit; marathon sessions are events. The monthly mock closes the loop — it measures whether the daily work is compounding or just accumulating.

pitfalls: Cramming. Fluency needs months of daily contact.
No error log. Repeating mistakes is the default; the log breaks it.
Skipping mental math. The interview's first filter is speed.
lessons.try_it: Start the error log today; enter your first three mistakes from the orientation scenarios.

lessons.title: Course Roadmap: The 15 Rungs
concepts: Rungs 1-3 (probability, statistics, stochastic processes): the mathematical foundation. Everything prices, hedges, and infers with these tools. Weak here = weak everywhere.
Rungs 4-6 (derivatives pricing, risk management, portfolio theory): the finance core — no-arbitrage pricing, measuring risk, building portfolios. The interview's center of gravity.
Rungs 7-9 (time series, Monte Carlo, ML for quant): the computational toolkit — modeling dynamics, simulating payoffs, learning from data. The practitioner's edge.
Rungs 10-12 (interview prep, capstone, mock assessment): the proving ground — the game, the project, the exam. Plus this orientation and the prerequisite audit in the ladder domain.

example.code:
The dependency graph:
  probability -> statistics -> stochastic processes -> derivatives pricing
  probability -> statistics -> ML for quant
  stochastic processes -> Monte Carlo -> derivatives pricing
  statistics -> time series -> risk management
  derivatives + risk + portfolio -> capstone
  ALL -> interview prep -> mock assessment
  Follow the arrows. Skipping ahead borrows confusion at interest.
example.walkthrough: The graph matters because confusion compounds: struggling with Black-Scholes is usually struggling with Itô's lemma, which is usually struggling with conditional expectation. When stuck, climb DOWN the graph to the weak rung, repair it, then climb back up.

pitfalls: Starting at derivatives. The graph says probability first.
Treating rungs as independent. They're a dependency graph.
Rushing the foundations. Weak foundations = weak everything.
lessons.try_it: Draw the dependency graph from memory; mark your weakest rung.

lessons.title: Terminal and Lab Guide
concepts: The labs run in Python: numpy, scipy, pandas, matplotlib, statsmodels, arch, scikit-learn. Install once: pip install numpy scipy pandas matplotlib statsmodels arch scikit-learn. Verify with the check script below.

Lab discipline: one directory per lab, a README with the objective, scripts named for their purpose, and outputs saved (figures, numbers). The checks in each lab are executable — run them; green means done.
Random seeds: set them (default_rng(42)) for reproducibility — but validate across seeds (the seed-picking lesson). Reproducible AND robust.
Getting help: the error log first (is this a repeat?), then the lesson's pitfalls, then documentation. Ask precise questions: 'my binomial price is 7.9 vs expected 7.19' beats 'it doesn't work.'

example.walkthrough: The check script is the gate: every lab assumes this stack. The seed discipline (set for reproducibility, vary for robustness) prevents the two failure modes — unreproducible results and seed-picked illusions. Precise questions get precise answers; 'it doesn't work' gets silence.

pitfalls: No environment check. Install first, debug never.
Unseeded randomness. Unreproducible labs can't be graded — even by you.
Vague help requests. Precise errors get precise fixes.
lessons.try_it: Run the environment check; fix any MISSING packages before lab 1.

lessons.title: Capstone Phase 1: Data and Pricing Engine
concepts: The project: a single Python platform that ingests option quotes, builds a vol surface, prices exotics by Monte Carlo, backtests a strategy, and reports risk. The interview artifact and the skill proof.

Phase 1 — data layer: fetch/store option chains (or use provided CSVs), clean quotes (arbitrage bounds!), timestamp everything point-in-time. The data layer is the foundation; garbage here poisons everything downstream.

Phase 1 — pricing engine: Black-Scholes (verified 10.4506), binomial trees (American), Monte Carlo with variance reduction (Asian/barrier). Each pricer unit-tested against known values — the test suite IS the credibility.
Deliverable: a repo with data/, pricers/, tests/ (all green), and a README. The README explains the architecture — interviewers read it first.

example.code:
Phase 1 checklist:
  [ ] option-chain ingest + cleaning (arb-bounds filter)
  [ ] BS pricer (test: 10.4506) + Greeks (test: closed forms)
  [ ] binomial tree (test: converges to BS; American >= European)
  [ ] MC engine (test: Asian vs approximation; SE reported)
  [ ] full test suite green; README with architecture
  Tests are the spec. Green suite = working platform.
example.walkthrough: The test-first discipline is what separates the capstone from a notebook: each pricer has known-value tests (10.4506, parity, tree convergence), so regressions are caught instantly. Interviewers trust tested code; untested code is a claim. The README's architecture section proves systems thinking, not just math.

pitfalls: Untested pricers. Known values exist; test against them.
Dirty data. Arb-violating quotes poison the surface.
No README. The architecture story is half the interview value.
lessons.try_it: Set up the repo; get the BS pricer tested to 10.4506.

lessons.title: Capstone Phase 2: Vol Surface and Risk
concepts: Phase 2 — vol surface: robust IV inversion (bounds-checked), smile construction, arbitrage validation (calendar + butterfly), constrained interpolation. The surface feeds every exotic price.

Phase 2 — risk engine: VaR (three methods, backtested), expected shortfall, stress scenarios (historical + reverse), Greeks aggregation across the book. Risk on the same platform as pricing — the professional setup.
The integration test: price a book of 20 options, compute total Greeks, VaR, and a stress scenario — one command, one report. The platform earns its name when the pieces compose.
Deliverable: surface/ and risk/ modules, the book-level report, and a write-up of every arbitrage violation found in the raw data (there will be some — documenting them shows market literacy).

example.code:
# book-level risk report (the integration test):
# book = list of (pricer, params, quantity)
# report = {
#   'pv': sum(qty * price),
#   'greeks': {'delta': ..., 'gamma': ..., 'vega': ..., 'theta': ...},
#   'var99_1d': historical_var(book_pnl),
#   'es99_1d': expected_shortfall(book_pnl),
#   'stress_2008': apply_shock(book, historical_2008),
# }
# One command -> one report. That's the platform.
print('Phase 2: surface + risk -> the book report')
example.walkthrough: The one-command report is the capstone's thesis: pricing, vol, and risk composed into a single artifact — exactly what a trading desk's system does. The arbitrage-violation write-up is a subtle signal: it shows you touched real data and know its dirt. Clean textbook data never teaches that; the capstone should.

pitfalls: Surface without arb checks. Violations price phantom edge.
Risk separate from pricing. One platform; compose them.
No stress scenarios. VaR alone is the weather forecast.
lessons.try_it: Build the IV inverter with bounds checking; document the first arb violation found.

lessons.title: Capstone Phase 3: Strategy Backtest and Validation
concepts: Phase 3 — strategy: pick ONE (skew trading, pairs, vol arbitrage) — implement the signal, the execution model (costs!), and the walk-forward backtest. One strategy done honestly beats five done hopefully.

Phase 3 — validation: the six-check audit (point-in-time, costs, walk-forward, baseline, regimes, replication-attempt). The backtest report leads with net-of-costs walk-forward Sharpe — the honest number first.

The final artifacts: the repo (tested), the backtest report (honest), a 10-minute walkthrough (record it), and a one-page summary (for the interviewer who won't read the repo). Four artifacts, four audiences.
The interview use: 'walk me through a project' → the capstone, STAR-structured, with the math you chose and the validation that humbled it. The project IS the fit-round answer.

example.code:
Phase 3 checklist:
  [ ] ONE strategy, fully specified (signal -> execution -> costs)
  [ ] walk-forward backtest (purged); net Sharpe reported first
  [ ] six-check audit written up (failures documented, not hidden)
  [ ] 10-min recorded walkthrough + one-page summary
  [ ] repo README: architecture, tests, how to run
  Honesty is the differentiator. Documented failures beat hidden ones.
example.walkthrough: The 'one strategy done honestly' constraint is the wisdom: breadth signals dilettantism, depth signals craft. The documented failures are the strongest interview signal — they prove you ran the audit on yourself. Interviewers have seen a hundred inflated backtests; they've rarely seen an honest one.

pitfalls: Five strategies, none validated. Depth over breadth.
Hiding the failures. The audit found them; report them.
No walkthrough. The recording is the interview rehearsal.
lessons.try_it: Pick your ONE strategy; write its specification (signal, execution, costs).

lessons.title: Quantitative Finance: The Prerequisite Audit
concepts: The audit is the highest-ROI study activity: rate yourself 0-3 on probability, statistics, linear algebra, calculus, and programming. The weakest area gets the most hours — study is triage, not tourism.

The bar: top quant interviews assume fluency in conditional expectation, Bayes, common distributions, linear algebra (eigen!), and stochastic thinking. 'Familiar' is not 'fluent' — fluency means deriving under pressure.
Programming is non-negotiable: Python (numpy/pandas) for modeling, plus C++ awareness for HFT-adjacent roles. The interview may ask you to code the model, not just state it.
Re-audit monthly: the ledger tracks which weaknesses closed and which persist. The audit is a living document, not a one-time quiz.

example.code:
Audit rubric (0-3):
  0: never seen it | 1: seen, can't use | 2: can use with notes
  3: fluent under pressure (derive + code + mental math)
  Target: all 2+ before rung 2; all 3 in your interview topics.
  Schedule: weakest-first, 60% of study time on sub-2 areas.
example.walkthrough: The rubric's honesty is the point: '2 with notes' is not interview-ready. The 60% rule forces the uncomfortable work — studying strengths feels productive and isn't.

pitfalls: Auditing once. Skills decay; re-audit monthly.
Studying strengths. Comfortable and useless.
Skipping programming. The model you can't code is a rumor.
lessons.try_it: Run the audit this week; publish your sub-2 list and schedule.

lessons.title: Quantitative Finance: The Career Fork
concepts: The fork: sell-side (bank trading, structuring), buy-side (hedge funds, asset managers), market-making (HFT/prop), and tech-adjacent (fintech, data). Different math, different interviews, different lives.
Sell-side quants: derivatives pricing, risk, regulatory models — deep stochastic calculus, slower pace. Buy-side: alpha research, portfolio construction — statistics and ML, P&L pressure.
Market makers: microstructure, low latency, probability at speed — the fastest interviews (mental math, games). The math is simpler; the speed is brutal.
Choose by temperament: deep math + stability (sell-side), research + risk (buy-side), speed + competition (market-making). The ladder serves all three; the interview prep tilts by fork.

example.code:
Fork map:
  SELL-SIDE: pricing/risk | interview: stoch calc, PDE, brainteasers
  BUY-SIDE: alpha/portfolio | interview: stats, ML, research taste
  MARKET-MAKING: microstructure | interview: mental math, games, probability
  Your prep weights follow your fork. Pick by temperament, not prestige.
example.walkthrough: The fork matters because interview prep is finite: market-making wants 30-second mental math; sell-side wants the PDE derivation. Preparing for all three equally prepares for none.

pitfalls: Chasing prestige over fit. The wrong fork is a short career.
Generic prep. Tilt by fork.
Ignoring the lifestyle. P&L pressure is real; know thyself.
lessons.try_it: Pick your fork tentatively; weight your interview prep accordingly.

lessons.title: Quantitative Finance: Reading Academic Papers
concepts: Papers are the field's source code: read for the model (assumptions), the result (theorem), and the gap (what's assumed away). Most interviews reference classic results — know the originals.
The reading method: abstract → model setup → main result → assumptions list. Skip proofs on first pass; return for the proof technique if the result matters to you.
Build a paper ledger: one line per paper (model, key result, key assumption, your critique). Fifty papers in the ledger is a literature education; the critique column is the interview value.
Start with the canon: Black-Scholes-Merton, Markowitz, Sharpe/CAPM, Fama-French, Engle (ARCH), Vasicek. The interviews assume these; the field builds on them.

example.code:
Paper ledger entry:
  PAPER: Black-Scholes (1973)
  MODEL: GBM, constant vol, no arbitrage, continuous hedging
  RESULT: PDE + closed form; risk-neutral pricing
  ASSUMPTION GAP: constant vol (smile!), continuous trading (costs!)
  CRITIQUE: the gaps ARE the subsequent literature (stoch vol, etc.)
example.walkthrough: The assumption-gap column is where interviews live: 'what breaks if vol isn't constant?' is a paper-ledger question. Reading for gaps turns consumption into critique.

pitfalls: Reading proofs first. Model and assumptions first; proofs later.
No ledger. Read-and-forget is entertainment, not education.
Only textbooks. Papers are where the field actually is.
lessons.try_it: Start the ledger with Black-Scholes; fill all five columns.

lessons.title: Quantitative Finance: The Interview Game
concepts: The game has three events: mental math/probability (speed), modeling (derivations, assumptions), and fit (why quant, why us). Train each separately; they use different muscles.
Mental math protocol: daily 15-minute drills (expected values, Bayes, normal approximations, quick arithmetic). Speed is trained, not gifted — the ledger tracks your times.
Modeling protocol: whiteboard derivations (Black-Scholes sketch, binomial tree, Bayes) narrated aloud. The narration is graded — silent derivation is a fail even if correct.
Fit protocol: know the firm's business (what do they trade?), have a market view (what's interesting now?), and a story (why you). Generic enthusiasm fits no desk.

example.code:
Daily drill (15 min):
  5 min: mental arithmetic (products, fractions, %s)
  5 min: probability puzzles (Bayes, EV, conditional)
  5 min: one derivation aloud (binomial price / BS sketch)
  Weekly: one full mock (90 min, interview conditions)
  The drill is the sport; the mock is the game.
example.walkthrough: The drill's separation is deliberate: arithmetic speed, puzzle pattern-matching, and derivation fluency are different skills. Training them together muddles; training them separately compounds.

pitfalls: Cramming the week before. Fluency needs months.
Silent practice. The interview is narrated; practice narrated.
No firm research. 'Why us?' needs a real answer.
lessons.try_it: Start the daily drill today; log your times.

lessons.title: Quantitative Finance: Common Pitfalls
concepts: Lookahead bias: using future information in backtests/decisions. The #1 empirical sin — point-in-time discipline always.
Survivorship bias: testing on survivors (current index members) inflates results. Use point-in-time universes; the dead stocks matter.
Overfitting: complex models on limited data — in-sample brilliance, out-of-sample failure. Prefer simple, validate out-of-sample, walk forward.
P vs Q confusion: pricing with real-world drift, forecasting with risk-neutral. 'Price' → Q; 'forecast' → P. The canonical theory error.
Ignoring costs: frictionless backtests are fiction. Model spread, slippage, fees from day one — they change the optimal strategy.

example.code:
Pitfall checklist (every model, every backtest):
  [ ] point-in-time data? (no lookahead)
  [ ] survivorship handled? (dead assets included)
  [ ] out-of-sample validated? (not just in-sample)
  [ ] P vs Q correct? (pricing->Q, forecasting->P)
  [ ] costs modeled? (spread+slippage+fees)
  Five checks; each catches a classic blowup.
example.walkthrough: The checklist is the pre-flight: run it on every model before trusting it. Each item is a famous disaster class — the checklist converts history into prevention.

pitfalls: Assuming your backtest is clean. Run the checklist.
Complexity as sophistication. Simple + validated beats complex + fit.
Forgetting costs. Net of costs or it didn't happen.
lessons.try_it: Run the checklist on your capstone backtester; fix the first failure.

lessons.title: Quantitative Finance: The Math You Must Own
concepts: Probability: conditional expectation (tower property!), Bayes, common distributions (normal, lognormal, binomial, Poisson), CLT, LLN. The working vocabulary.
Linear algebra: eigenvalues/eigenvectors (PCA, stability), matrix decompositions (Cholesky for correlated simulation), projections (regression geometry). Quants live in vector spaces.
Calculus: Taylor expansions (Greeks are Taylors!), Itô's lemma (the chain rule of stochastic calculus), PDEs (Black-Scholes). The continuous-time machinery.
Statistics: estimation (MLE), hypothesis testing, regression — and their limits (p-hacking, multiple testing). The inference toolkit with its warning labels.

example.code:
Own = derive + compute + code:
  DERIVE: tower property, Bayes, BS PDE sketch, CAPM
  COMPUTE: by hand — binomial price, Bayes update, eigenvalues 2x2
  CODE: numpy implementations of each (labs)
  'Own' means all three. Two out of three is studying; three is owning.
example.walkthrough: The three-mode definition is the standard: derivation (understanding), hand computation (fluency), implementation (working knowledge). Interviews test all three — often in the same question.

pitfalls: Derivation without computation. The algebra must work by hand.
Code without derivation. The library call isn't understanding.
Skipping linear algebra. Eigenvalues are everywhere in quant.
lessons.try_it: Self-test: derive the tower property, compute a 2x2 eigen-decomposition by hand, code it.

lessons.title: Axioms and Conditional Probability
concepts: Kolmogorov's axioms: P(A) >= 0, P(Omega) = 1, countable additivity for disjoint events. Everything follows — including the things people get wrong.
Conditional probability: P(A|B) = P(A,B)/P(B) — restrict the universe to B, renormalize. 'Given B' means B happened; update the sample space.
Law of total probability: P(A) = sum P(A|Bi)P(Bi) over a partition. The workhorse for 'compute via cases' — every Bayes denominator uses it.
Independence: P(A,B) = P(A)P(B) — AND the conditional version. Uncorrelated is not independent (only for normal); independent is the strong claim. Interviews probe this.

example.code:
# conditional probability by counting (the honest way):
import itertools
omega = list(itertools.product([1,2,3,4,5,6], repeat=2))  # two dice
A = [w for w in omega if sum(w) == 9]      # sum is 9
B = [w for w in omega if w[0] == 3]          # first die is 3
print(len([w for w in A if w in B]) / len(B))  # P(A|B) = 1/6
# B has 6 outcomes; only (3,6) sums to 9 -> 1/6. Count, don't guess.
example.walkthrough: Counting makes conditional probability concrete: restrict to B (6 outcomes), count A within (1). The formula P(A,B)/P(B) = (1/36)/(6/36) = 1/6 agrees. When confused, enumerate — small cases reveal the structure.

pitfalls: P(A|B) vs P(B|A). The direction matters enormously (prosecutor's fallacy).
Assuming independence. Check it; don't feel it.
Uncorrelated = independent. False except for jointly normal.
lessons.try_it: Compute P(sum=9 | first die odd) by counting; verify with the formula.

lessons.title: Bayes' Theorem
concepts: Bayes: P(H|E) = P(E|H)P(H)/P(E) — update beliefs with evidence. Posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence. The single most interview-tested formula.
The denominator via total probability: P(E) = P(E|H)P(H) + P(E|not H)P(not H). Forgetting the second term is the classic error — the evidence must be normalized over all hypotheses.
Base rates dominate: rare diseases stay rare even after positive tests (the 16.7% example). Intuition ignores priors; Bayes doesn't. Every 'surprising' Bayes result is the prior talking.
Odds form: posterior odds = likelihood ratio × prior odds. Cleaner for sequential updates — multiply the ratios as evidence arrives. Quants update; they don't restart.

example.code:
# disease test: 1% prevalence, 99% sensitivity, 95% specificity
p_d, sens, spec = 0.01, 0.99, 0.95
p_pos = sens*p_d + (1-spec)*(1-p_d)   # total prob of positive
posterior = sens*p_d / p_pos
print(f'P(disease|+) = {posterior:.3f}')  # 0.167, NOT 0.99
# intuition says 99%; Bayes says 16.7%. The prior (1%) dominates.
example.walkthrough: The 16.7% is the lesson: P(+|disease)=99% feels like certainty, but most positives are false (5% of the 99% healthy). Bayes forces the base rate into the calculation — intuition skips it. Verify: 0.0099/(0.0099+0.0495)=0.1667. Correct.

pitfalls: P(E|H) for P(H|E). The prosecutor's fallacy — the interview classic.
Dropping the denominator's second term. Normalize over ALL hypotheses.
Ignoring base rates. Rare stays rare-ish.
lessons.try_it: Compute P(disease|+) for prevalence 0.1%: watch the posterior collapse.

lessons.title: Random Variables and Expectation
concepts: Random variable: a function X: Omega → R. Discrete (pmf sums to 1) vs continuous (pdf integrates to 1). The distribution is the object; the variable is the mapping.
Expectation: E[X] = sum x·p(x) (discrete) or integral x·f(x)dx. Linearity: E[aX+bY] = aE[X]+bE[Y] — NO independence needed. The most-used theorem in quant.
Variance: Var(X) = E[X²] - E[X]² = E[(X-E[X])²]. For independent: Var(sum) = sum of Vars. Standard deviation is the square root — the units matter.
Tower property: E[E[X|Y]] = E[X] — iterated expectations collapse. The quant's hammer: condition on what you know, then uncondition. Used constantly in pricing.

example.code:
import numpy as np
# linearity needs NO independence:
# E[sum of dice] = sum of E[die] = 2 * 3.5 = 7.0
# variance of sum (independent): 2 * 35/12 = 5.833
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
s = rng.integers(1, 7, size=(10**6, 2)).sum(axis=1)
print(s.mean(), s.var())  # ~7.0, ~5.83: simulation confirms theory
example.walkthrough: The simulation confirms both: mean 7.0 (linearity) and variance 5.83 (sum of independent variances). Theory predicts; Monte Carlo verifies — the quant workflow in miniature. Note Var(die)=35/12≈2.917; doubled ≈5.833. Correct.

pitfalls: E[XY] = E[X]E[Y] without independence. False in general.
Var(aX) = a·Var(X). It's a² — the classic slip.
Forgetting the tower property. Condition, compute, collapse.
lessons.try_it: Prove Var(aX+b) = a²Var(X) from the definition; verify by simulation.

lessons.title: Essential Distributions
concepts: Normal N(mu, sigma²): the limit of everything (CLT). 68-95-99.7 rule. Lognormal: exp of normal — the stock price model (positive, skewed). Know both cold.

Binomial(n,p): k successes in n trials. Poisson(lambda): rare events per interval — the limit of Binomial(n, lambda/n). Exponential: waiting time, memoryless — the ONLY memoryless continuous distribution.
Memoryless property: P(X > s+t | X > s) = P(X > t) — for exponential (continuous) and geometric (discrete). 'How long you've waited tells you nothing' — queuing and default modeling use this.

CLT: sample means → normal as n grows, regardless of the underlying distribution (finite variance). The justification for normal approximations everywhere — and the reason 'n=30' appears in textbooks.

example.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
# CLT demo: means of exponential samples -> normal
means = [rng.exponential(scale=2.0, size=1000).mean() for _ in range(5000)]
print(np.mean(means), np.std(means))  # ~2.0, ~0.063 = 2/sqrt(1000)
# exponential mean=2, sd=2; mean-of-1000 has sd 2/sqrt(1000)=0.0632. Correct.
example.walkthrough: The CLT demo's numbers verify the theory: the sampling distribution's sd is sigma/sqrt(n) = 2/31.62 = 0.0632, matching simulation. This is why Monte Carlo error shrinks as 1/sqrt(N) — same theorem, financial application.

pitfalls: Normal for everything. Check skew/tails first — lognormal for prices.
Poisson for non-rare events. It's the rare-event limit.
Forgetting memoryless is exponential-only. Normal is NOT memoryless.
lessons.try_it: Verify the 68-95-99.7 rule by simulation; then break it with a lognormal.

lessons.title: Joint Distributions and Conditioning
concepts: Joint, marginal, conditional: p(x,y) → p(x) = sum_y p(x,y) (marginalize) → p(x|y) = p(x,y)/p(y) (condition). The three moves; everything else is bookkeeping.
Covariance and correlation: Cov(X,Y) = E[XY]-E[X]E[Y]; rho = Cov/(sigma_x sigma_y), in [-1,1]. Correlation measures LINEAR association — zero correlation ≠ independence (except jointly normal).
Conditional expectation E[X|Y]: a random variable (function of Y), the best predictor of X given Y (minimizes MSE). Regression IS conditional expectation estimation.
Bivariate normal: the workhorse — linear conditionals, everything closed-form. If (X,Y) jointly normal, E[X|Y=y] is linear in y. Portfolio math lives here.

example.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
# correlated normals via Cholesky: the simulation workhorse
rho = 0.6
L = np.linalg.cholesky([[1, rho], [rho, 1]])
z = rng.standard_normal((2, 10**6))
x, y = L @ z
print(np.corrcoef(x, y)[0,1])  # ~0.6: Cholesky imposes the correlation
# E[X|Y=y] = rho*y (standardized): verify by binning
example.walkthrough: Cholesky is how quants simulate correlated assets: L·z has covariance LL' = Sigma. The construction is exact — LL' reproduces the target correlation matrix. Verify: np.corrcoef gives 0.6. This pattern appears in every Monte Carlo pricer with multiple underlyings.

pitfalls: Zero correlation = independence. Only for jointly normal.
E[X|Y] as a number. It's a random variable (function of Y).
Marginalizing wrong. Sum/integrate out the RIGHT variable.
lessons.try_it: Simulate correlated normals; verify E[X|Y=y] ≈ rho*y by binning.

lessons.title: Estimators: Bias, Variance, MLE
concepts: Estimator quality: bias (E[theta_hat] - theta; systematic error), variance (sampling noise), MSE = bias² + variance. The bias-variance trade-off governs model complexity.

MLE: choose theta maximizing P(data|theta) — equivalently maximize log-likelihood (sums beat products). Asymptotically unbiased, efficient (Cramér-Rao), and normal. The default estimator for a reason.
Sample variance: divide by n-1 (Bessel's correction) for unbiasedness — one degree lost estimating the mean. MLE divides by n (biased but consistent). Know which your library uses.

Consistency (converges to truth as n→∞) vs unbiasedness (right on average at finite n). Consistency is the guarantee that matters; unbiasedness is nice. MLE has the first always, the second asymptotically.

example.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
x = rng.normal(loc=5, scale=2, size=1000)
# MLE normal: mean=x.mean(), var=((x-x.mean())**2).mean()  (divides by n)
# unbiased var: x.var(ddof=1)  (divides by n-1)
print(x.mean(), x.var(), x.var(ddof=1))  # ~5.0, ~3.99, ~4.00
# true var=4: MLE slightly low (biased), ddof=1 unbiased. Both consistent.
example.walkthrough: The ddof=1 correction is Bessel's: estimating the mean from the same data costs one degree of freedom. At n=1000 the difference is trivial; at n=5 it's decisive. Know your n.

pitfalls: Unbiased = best. MSE (bias²+var) is the criterion; biased can win.
MLE always unbiased. Only asymptotically.
Ignoring ddof. Libraries differ; check.
lessons.try_it: Estimate normal params by MLE on simulated data; compare ddof=0 vs 1 at n=10.

lessons.title: Hypothesis Testing Done Right
concepts: The framework: H0 (null) vs H1, test statistic, p-value = P(data this extreme | H0). p < 0.05 rejects H0 — it does NOT prove H1, and it's not P(H0 false).
Errors: Type I (false positive, alpha) vs Type II (false negative, beta); power = 1 - beta. You choose alpha; power comes from n and effect size. Underpowered tests are coin flips with extra steps.
p-hacking: testing 20 strategies, one 'works' at p=0.05 by chance. Multiple testing needs correction (Bonferroni: alpha/20) or out-of-sample validation. Most 'significant' findings are this.
Confidence intervals > p-values: 'effect is 2.1 ± 0.3' beats 'p < 0.05'. CIs show magnitude AND uncertainty; p-values collapse both into a threshold. Report intervals.

example.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
# strategy returns vs 0: is the mean positive?
rets = rng.normal(loc=0.001, scale=0.02, size=252)  # tiny edge, 1yr daily
t, p = stats.ttest_1samp(rets, 0)
print(f't={t:.2f}, p={p:.3f}')  # likely NOT significant: power too low
# need ~4x data for this edge: power analysis before the test, not after
example.walkthrough: The power lesson: a real edge (0.001 daily ≈ 28% annualized!) is undetectable in 1 year of daily data at 5% significance. Power analysis BEFORE testing tells you the required n; after is regret. Most quant 'insignificance' is underpower, not absence.

pitfalls: p = P(H0 false). It's P(data|H0) — the inverse fallacy.
Testing 20 variants at 0.05. Bonferroni or out-of-sample.
'Not significant' = 'no effect.' Underpowered ≠ absent.
lessons.try_it: Power analysis: what n detects Sharpe 1.0 at 80% power? Compute it.

lessons.title: Regression: The Workhorse
concepts: OLS: beta_hat = (X'X)^-1 X'y — the projection of y onto X's column space. Geometric, closed-form, and the best linear unbiased estimator (Gauss-Markov, given the assumptions).

Assumptions that matter: linearity, exogeneity (E[e|X]=0 — the big one; violated by omitted variables), homoskedasticity (for standard errors), no perfect collinearity. Violations don't bias beta_hat (except exogeneity) but break inference.
R² is not goodness: high R² with wrong model is still wrong; low R² with the right model is honest. Out-of-sample R² is the only one that counts for prediction.
Regularization: ridge (L2, shrinks), lasso (L1, selects). The bias-variance trade made explicit — trading a little bias for a lot less variance. Cross-validate the penalty.

example.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
X = rng.normal(size=(1000, 3)); true_b = np.array([1.0, -2.0, 0.5])
y = X @ true_b + rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=1000)
beta = np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X) @ X.T @ y
print(beta)  # ~[1, -2, 0.5]: OLS recovers truth (Gauss-Markov)
# omitted variable: drop X[:,2] from regression -> bias in the rest
example.walkthrough: The omitted-variable demo is the exogeneity lesson: drop a correlated regressor and the remaining coefficients absorb its effect — biased, and no standard error warns you. This is why 'control for everything relevant' isn't advice, it's identification.

pitfalls: R² worship. Out-of-sample or it didn't happen.
Ignoring exogeneity. Omitted variables bias everything.
No regularization with many features. Overfit by default.
lessons.try_it: Regress with an omitted correlated variable; measure the bias.

lessons.title: Bayesian Inference
concepts: Bayes for parameters: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. The prior is your belief before data; the posterior is the update. Sequential updating is built in — yesterday's posterior is today's prior.
Conjugate priors (Beta-Binomial, Normal-Normal): closed-form posteriors. The Beta(α,β) prior + Binomial data → Beta(α+k, β+n-k) posterior. Interview-friendly and genuinely useful.
Priors matter most with little data; wash out with much (Bernstein-von Mises). The 'subjective' critique bites at n=10, not n=10,000. Report prior sensitivity.
MCMC for the hard cases: when no conjugacy, sample the posterior (Metropolis-Hastings, NUTS). Convergence diagnostics (R-hat) are mandatory — unmixed chains lie confidently.

example.code:
# Beta-Binomial: coin bias with prior Beta(2,2) (weakly favors 0.5)
# observe 8 heads in 10 flips -> posterior Beta(2+8, 2+2) = Beta(10,4)
# posterior mean = 10/14 = 0.714; MLE = 0.8; prior pulls toward 0.5
alpha, beta, k, n = 2, 2, 8, 10
post_mean = (alpha+k)/(alpha+beta+n)
print(post_mean)  # 0.714: prior (2,2) + data (8/10) -> compromise
# with n=1000, k=800: 802/1004 = 0.799: data dominates. Correct.
example.walkthrough: The numbers show the prior's role: at n=10, prior pulls 0.8→0.714; at n=1000, 0.800→0.799 — data swamps prior. This is the honest answer to 'aren't priors subjective?': they matter exactly when data is scarce, which is when you need them most.

pitfalls: Flat priors = 'objective.' They're still choices (and improper ones break).
Ignoring convergence. Unmixed MCMC is confident nonsense.
Point estimates from posteriors without intervals. The distribution IS the answer.
lessons.try_it: Beta-Binomial updating: start Beta(1,1), update flip by flip, watch the posterior narrow.

lessons.title: Inference Pitfalls for Quants
concepts: Multiple testing: 1000 strategies backtested, 50 'significant' at 5% — expected by chance alone. Corrections (Bonferroni, FDR) or out-of-sample. The quant version of p-hacking is strategy-mining.
Overfitting: in-sample Sharpe 3, out-of-sample 0. The defense: simple models, walk-forward validation, and the 'too good' prior (deflated Sharpe ratios). Complexity must earn its keep out-of-sample.
Non-stationarity: markets change regimes; parameters estimated on 2019 data may not hold in 2024. Rolling estimation and regime awareness — the past is a guide, not a guarantee.
Publication/selection bias: you see the strategies that worked (yours, papers'). The file drawer is full of failures. Discount everything by the selection process that surfaced it.

example.code:
Validation ladder:
  1. in-sample fit (necessary, not sufficient)
  2. out-of-sample (one shot, pre-registered)
  3. walk-forward (rolling re-estimation)
  4. paper trade (live data, no capital)
  5. small capital (real friction)
  Each rung kills false positives. Skipping rungs kills capital.
example.walkthrough: The ladder's discipline is sequential honesty: each rung is a chance for the strategy to die cheaply. Strategies that skip to live trading skip their autopsy — and become someone else's cautionary tale.

pitfalls: In-sample worship. The only test that matters is out-of-sample.
One backtest, full capital. The ladder exists for a reason.
Ignoring regime change. 2019 parameters, 2024 markets.
lessons.try_it: Take a known-good strategy; run the full validation ladder and document each rung.

lessons.title: Random Walks and Brownian Motion
concepts: Random walk: S_n = sum of iid steps — the discrete ancestor. Symmetric simple random walk: ±1 steps, E[S_n]=0, Var(S_n)=n. Variance grows linearly with time — the seed of everything.
Brownian motion (Wiener process): continuous-time limit — W_0=0, independent increments, W_t - W_s ~ N(0, t-s), continuous paths. The variance-scaling (Var(W_t)=t) is the signature.
Scaling property: W_{ct} has the same distribution as sqrt(c)·W_t — zoom in and it looks the same (fractal). This self-similarity is why the same math works at all timescales.
Reflection principle and friends: P(max W > a) = 2P(W_t > a) — barrier probabilities in closed form. The tools for barrier options start here.

example.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(6)
# Brownian motion: cumulative sum of N(0, dt) increments
T, N = 1.0, 1000
dt = T/N
dW = rng.normal(scale=np.sqrt(dt), size=N)  # Var = dt per step
W = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(dW)])
print(W[-1], W[-1]**2)  # W_T ~ N(0,1); E[W_T^2] = T = 1
# Var scales with t: the increment sd is sqrt(dt), NOT dt. Correct.
example.walkthrough: The sqrt(dt) scaling is THE point: variance adds linearly (Var = t), so standard deviation scales as sqrt(t). Using dt instead of sqrt(dt) is the classic simulation bug — it produces the wrong volatility by a factor of sqrt(dt).

pitfalls: Increment sd = dt. It's sqrt(dt) — variance linear in time.
Forgetting W_0 = 0. Paths start at zero.
Assuming differentiability. Brownian paths are nowhere differentiable.
lessons.try_it: Simulate 10k paths; verify Var(W_1) ≈ 1 and the reflection principle numerically.

lessons.title: Martingales: Fair Games
concepts: Martingale: E[M_{t+1} | F_t] = M_t — the best prediction of tomorrow is today. Fair games, and (under Q) discounted asset prices. The no-arbitrage condition in probability language.
Examples: symmetric random walk, Brownian motion, and — crucially — discounted stock prices under the risk-neutral measure. 'No free lunch' = 'discounted prices are Q-martingales.'
Optional stopping: E[M_tau] = E[M_0] for bounded stopping times — you can't beat a fair game by clever stopping. The math behind 'no trading strategy creates arbitrage.'
Doob's inequalities bound the maximum: P(max M > a) <= E[M_T]/a. Maximum drawdown and barrier probabilities live here — risk management's probabilistic foundation.

example.code:
# discounted stock under Q is a martingale: E_Q[e^{-rT} S_T] = S_0
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
S0, r, sigma, T, N = 100, 0.05, 0.2, 1.0, 200000
Z = rng.standard_normal(N)
ST = S0 * np.exp((r - 0.5*sigma**2)*T + sigma*np.sqrt(T)*Z)  # GBM under Q
print(np.exp(-r*T) * ST.mean())  # ~100 = S0: martingale verified
# drift r (not mu!) makes the discounted price a martingale. Correct.
example.walkthrough: The verification IS the fundamental theorem in action: under Q (drift r), the discounted stock's expectation is today's price — no arbitrage. Change drift to mu and it fails: that's P, not Q. The measure is the message.

pitfalls: Martingale = constant. It's conditionally constant expectation — paths vary.
Optional stopping always. Needs boundedness/integrability — gambler's ruin breaks it.
Forgetting the measure. Martingale under Q, not necessarily under P.
lessons.try_it: Verify the martingale property for a symmetric random walk by simulation.

lessons.title: Itô Calculus
concepts: Itô's lemma: df = (f_t + mu f_x + ½σ²f_xx)dt + σf_x dW — the chain rule with a second-order correction. The ½σ²f_xx term is the entire difference from ordinary calculus, and the source of the BS PDE.

Why the correction: (dW)² = dt (quadratic variation) — Brownian motion accumulates variance linearly, so second-order terms don't vanish. Ordinary calculus assumes (dx)² = 0; stochastic calculus can't.
Itô integral: integral of H dW is a martingale (zero expectation) when H is adapted and square-integrable. Expectations of Itô integrals vanish — the computational workhorse.
Geometric Brownian motion: dS = mu S dt + sigma S dW → S_t = S_0 exp((mu - ½σ²)t + σW_t). The -½σ² is Itô's correction made visible — the median grows slower than the mean.

example.code:
# Itô correction visible: E[S_T] vs median(S_T) for GBM
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(8)
mu, sigma, T, S0, N = 0.08, 0.3, 1.0, 100, 500000
ST = S0*np.exp((mu-0.5*sigma**2)*T + sigma*np.sqrt(T)*rng.standard_normal(N))
print(ST.mean(), np.median(ST))  # mean ~108.3 (=100e^0.08), median ~103.6
# mean = S0*e^{mu*T} = 108.33; median = S0*e^{(mu-sig^2/2)*T} = 103.6. Correct.
example.walkthrough: The mean/median gap IS the Itô correction: the mean grows at mu (108.33 = 100·e^0.08), the median at mu - σ²/2 (103.6). Most paths underperform the mean — the distribution is right-skewed. This gap explains why 'expected return' misleads about typical outcomes.

pitfalls: Forgetting the ½σ² term. It's the whole ballgame.
E[int H dW] ≠ 0. It IS zero (martingale) — use it.
Confusing mean and median growth. Median lags by σ²/2.
lessons.try_it: Derive the GBM solution via Itô on f = ln S; verify mean/median by simulation.

lessons.title: SDEs in Finance: The Model Zoo
concepts: GBM: dS = mu S dt + sigma S dW — lognormal prices, constant vol. The Black-Scholes workhorse. Fails: vol smile, jumps, stochastic vol.
Mean-reverting (OU/Vasicek): dx = kappa(theta - x)dt + sigma dW — rates, spreads, volatility pull back to theta at speed kappa. Half-life = ln2/kappa. The quant's second model.
Stochastic vol (Heston): vol itself follows a CIR process — produces the smile. Two Brownian motions, correlation rho (leverage effect: negative rho = crash skew).
Jumps (Merton): GBM + Poisson jumps — fat tails, short-dated smile. Each extension fixes a Black-Scholes failure; each adds parameters to calibrate (and overfit).

example.code:
# Ornstein-Uhlenbeck: exact discretization
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
kappa, theta, sigma, x0, T, N = 2.0, 0.05, 0.02, 0.03, 1.0, 252
dt = T/N
x = np.zeros(N+1); x[0] = x0
for i in range(N):
    x[i+1] = x[i] + kappa*(theta-x[i])*dt + sigma*np.sqrt(dt)*rng.standard_normal()
print(x.mean(), x[-50:].mean())  # ~0.05: reverts to theta. Half-life ln2/2=0.35y
example.walkthrough: The OU simulation shows mean reversion: starting at 0.03, the path gravitates to theta=0.05 with half-life ln(2)/2 ≈ 0.35 years. The exact discretization is Euler here (fine for small dt); the point is the pullback term kappa(theta - x) — the only difference from Brownian motion, and it changes everything.

pitfalls: GBM for rates. Rates mean-revert; GBM doesn't.
Calibrating 6 parameters on 10 options. Overfit city.
Ignoring the model's failures. Every model is wrong; know how.
lessons.try_it: Simulate Heston vs GBM smiles: price OTM puts under each, compare implied vols.

lessons.title: Change of Measure: Girsanov
concepts: Girsanov: change the drift of a Brownian motion by changing the measure — W^Q_t = W^P_t - integral theta ds is Q-Brownian. Same paths, different probabilities.
The market price of risk: theta = (mu - r)/sigma — the Sharpe ratio per unit vol. Girsanov shifts drift by exactly this: under Q, everything drifts at r.
Why it matters: pricing doesn't need P at all — specify the model under Q directly (drift r, same vol). The real-world drift mu is unidentifiable from options and irrelevant to price.
Radon-Nikodym derivative: dQ/dP = exp(-½∫theta² + ∫theta dW) — the likelihood ratio reweighting paths. Monte Carlo under P reweighted to Q is valid but inefficient; simulate under Q directly.

example.code:
Girsanov in one line:
  Under P: dS = mu*S dt + sigma*S dW^P
  Define dW^Q = dW^P - ((mu-r)/sigma) dt  [shift by market price of risk]
  Under Q: dS = r*S dt + sigma*S dW^Q     [drift becomes r]
  Same volatility, different drift. Price under Q; forecast under P.
  The mu vanishes from pricing. That's the fundamental theorem.
example.walkthrough: The one-line version is the working knowledge: Girsanov is the machinery that makes 'drift = r' legitimate. You rarely compute Radon-Nikodym derivatives by hand — but knowing the drift shift IS Girsanov lets you move between measures fluently.

pitfalls: Pricing under P. The drift mu is irrelevant to arbitrage-free price.
Thinking Girsanov changes paths. Same paths, reweighted probabilities.
Forgetting vol is unchanged. Girsanov shifts drift, not diffusion.
lessons.try_it: Price an option by Monte Carlo under P with mu=12%, then under Q — compare.

lessons.title: No-Arbitrage and Replication
concepts: Arbitrage: riskless profit from nothing — the market's conservation law. Prices must exclude it; everything in derivatives follows from this one principle.
Replication: a derivative's price = cost of the replicating portfolio (delta shares + cash). If you can build the payoff from traded assets, the price is forced — no model needed, just no-arbitrage.
Law of one price: identical payoffs, identical prices. Put-call parity (C - P = S - Ke^{-rT}) is the purest example — model-free, from a static replication (long call + cash = long put + stock).
Static vs dynamic replication: parity is static (set and forget); Black-Scholes needs dynamic (continuous delta hedging). The more complete the market, the less model you need.

example.code:
# put-call parity: C - P = S - K*exp(-rT), model-free
S, K, r, T = 100, 100, 0.05, 1.0
# any consistent pricer must satisfy this; use it as a TEST:
# if your BS call=10.45, your put MUST be 10.45 - 100 + 100*exp(-0.05) = 5.57
rhs = S - K*np.exp(-r*T)
print(rhs)  # 4.877: C - P must equal this, whatever C and P are
example.walkthrough: The parity value 4.877 is model-free: any pricer violating it has an arbitrage (buy the cheap side, sell the dear). Use parity as a unit test for every pricer you write — it's the fastest way to catch bugs.

pitfalls: Pricing by 'expected payoff' under P. Discount Q-expectation.
Ignoring replication. Price = replication cost, always.
Forgetting parity as a test. It's the free unit test.
lessons.try_it: Prove put-call parity with the static portfolio; use it to test your BS code.

lessons.title: Binomial Trees
concepts: One step: S→{Su, Sd}; price = e^{-rΔt}[p·Cu + (1-p)·Cd], p = (e^{rΔt} - d)/(u - d). The risk-neutral p is FORCED by no-arbitrage (replication), not estimated — it's the p making the stock's expected return r.
Multi-step: build the tree forward, price backward (dynamic programming). n steps → converges to Black-Scholes as n→∞ (with u = e^{σ√Δt}). The tree IS the discrete BS.
American options: at each node, value = max(exercise, hold) — backward induction with the early-exercise check. Trees price Americans; closed forms (mostly) don't. This is the tree's killer app.
The p is not a forecast: p=0.75 doesn't mean '75% chance up' — it's the pricing weight. Confusing Q-probabilities with real ones is the canonical error.

example.code:
import numpy as np
# one-step binomial: S=100, K=100, u=1.1, d=0.9, r=5%
S, K, u, d, r = 100, 100, 1.1, 0.9, 0.05
p = (np.exp(r) - d)/(u - d)  # (1.0513-0.9)/0.2 = 0.7564
Cu, Cd = max(S*u-K, 0), max(S*d-K, 0)  # 10, 0
C = np.exp(-r)*(p*Cu + (1-p)*Cd)
print(p, C)  # 0.7564, 7.197: the no-arbitrage price. p is forced, not fit.
example.walkthrough: Check the arithmetic: e^0.05 = 1.05127; p = (1.05127-0.9)/(1.1-0.9) = 0.15127/0.2 = 0.75635. C = e^{-0.05} × 0.75635 × 10 = 0.95123 × 7.5635 = 7.194. The code prints ~7.19 — correct. Note p ≠ 0.5: the risk-neutral weight reflects the drift constraint, not real odds.

pitfalls: p as forecast. It's the replication weight.
u,d arbitrary. Match moments: u = e^{σ√Δt} for BS convergence.
Forgetting American check. max(exercise, hold) every node.
lessons.try_it: Price a 3-step American put by hand; verify against your code.

lessons.title: Black-Scholes Formula
concepts: The formula: C = S·N(d1) - K·e^{-rT}·N(d2); d1 = [ln(S/K) + (r + σ²/2)T]/(σ√T); d2 = d1 - σ√T. N(d2) ≈ Q(prob ITM); S·N(d1) is the replicating delta's present value.
Derivation sketch: Itô on the option value → delta-hedged portfolio is riskless → must earn r → BS PDE → solve (heat equation) → formula. The PDE is the no-arbitrage condition in continuous time.
Assumptions (know the failures): constant vol (smile!), continuous trading (costs!), no jumps (crash!), lognormal (tails!), constant r. Every extension (Heston, jumps, local vol) fixes one failure.
Put price via parity: P = C - S + Ke^{-rT}. Never code the put formula separately — parity is exact and halves your bug surface.

example.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm
def bs_call(S, K, T, r, sigma):
    d1 = (np.log(S/K) + (r + 0.5*sigma**2)*T)/(sigma*np.sqrt(T))
    d2 = d1 - sigma*np.sqrt(T)
    return S*norm.cdf(d1) - K*np.exp(-r*T)*norm.cdf(d2)
print(bs_call(100, 100, 1.0, 0.05, 0.2))  # 10.4506: the canonical ATM price
# put via parity: 10.4506 - 100 + 95.1229 = 5.5735. Verify: matches bs put.
example.walkthrough: The canonical value 10.4506 is the industry's 'hello world' — memorize it as a sanity check. Verify d1: ln(1)=0, (0.05+0.02)×1=0.07, /0.2 = 0.35; d2 = 0.15. N(0.35)=0.6368, N(0.15)=0.5596. C = 63.68 - 95.1229×0.5596 = 63.68-53.23 = 10.45. Correct.

pitfalls: Coding put separately. Use parity.
d1/d2 swapped. d1 has the +σ²/2; d2 = d1 - σ√T.
Forgetting assumptions. The formula is exact for a wrong model.
lessons.try_it: Implement bs_call; verify 10.4506 and parity-implied put 5.5735.

lessons.title: The Greeks
concepts: Delta (Δ=∂C/∂S=N(d1)): the hedge ratio — shares per option. Gamma (Γ=∂²C/∂S²): how fast delta changes; the hedging cost driver. Gamma scalping P&L ≈ ½ΓS²((dS/S)² - σ²dt).
Vega (∂C/∂σ): vol exposure — the biggest risk for most books. Theta (∂C/∂t, negative): time decay, the price of waiting. Rho: rate sensitivity (minor for most).
Taylor view: dC ≈ ΔdS + ½Γ(dS)² + Θdt + νdσ — the Greeks are the Taylor coefficients. Hedged P&L = gamma/theta trade-off: long gamma pays theta; the balance is fair at implied vol.
Second-order and cross Greeks (vanna, volga) matter for exotics and smile dynamics. First-order Greeks run vanilla books; the smile needs the second order.

example.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm
# Greeks by closed form (call): S=100,K=100,T=1,r=0.05,sig=0.2
d1 = 0.35; d2 = 0.15  # from the canonical example
Delta = norm.cdf(d1)  # 0.6368
Gamma = norm.pdf(d1)/(100*0.2)  # 0.01876
Vega = 100*norm.pdf(d1)*1.0  # 37.52 (per 1.0 vol; /100 for 1pt)
Theta = -(100*norm.pdf(d1)*0.2/2) - 0.05*100*np.exp(-0.05)*norm.cdf(d2)
print(Delta, Gamma, Vega, Theta)  # 0.6368, 0.0188, 37.52, -6.41/yr
example.walkthrough: Verify theta: -S·n(d1)·σ/(2√T) = -100×0.3752×0.2/2 = -3.752; -rKe^{-rT}N(d2) = -0.05×95.1229×0.5596 = -2.662. Sum: -6.414/yr ≈ -0.0176/day. Correct. The Greeks' signs: delta +, gamma +, vega +, theta − (long option decays).

pitfalls: Delta-hedging once. Hedge dynamically; gamma is the cost.
Ignoring vega. Vol moves are the book-killer.
Theta as 'free money.' Short options earn theta by bearing gamma risk.
lessons.try_it: Compute Greeks by bump-and-revalue; match closed forms to 1e-4.

lessons.title: Implied Volatility and the Smile
concepts: Implied vol: the σ making BS match the market price — the market's forecast, quoted in vol units. Invert BS numerically (bisection/Newton); vega > 0 guarantees uniqueness.
The smile: implied vol varies with strike — OTM puts (crash protection) trade rich. BS assumes flat; the market disagrees. The smile IS the market's rejection of lognormal/constant-vol.
Skew vs smile: equity index = skew (downside bid); FX = smile (both tails); the shape encodes the market's feared distribution. Read shapes, not just levels.
Vol surfaces: σ(K,T) — arbitrage-free constraints (calendar: total variance increasing in T; butterfly: density positive). Interpolating surfaces without violating these creates phantom arbitrage.

example.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm
from scipy.optimize import brentq
def bs_call(S,K,T,r,sig):
    d1=(np.log(S/K)+(r+0.5*sig**2)*T)/(sig*np.sqrt(T)); d2=d1-sig*np.sqrt(T)
    return S*norm.cdf(d1)-K*np.exp(-r*T)*norm.cdf(d2)
